You have told me, time and time again, that I am ignorant, childlike, and have a lot to learn.

I actually think it's you who needs to learn a few things, and unlike you, I will not be vague and woolly. I will be highly specific.

1. Empathy, Kindness and Perspective-Taking. Please see list of previously-shared sources.
2. What domestic abuse actually encompasses, and the various ways it can impact victims and survivors. Please refer to my first two posts, which cite sources such as the UK Government, a domestic abuse charity, and a Dive In event centering survivors of abuse.
3. What truth and facts are, and how to find, express, and cite them in your writing.
4. What a word salad is. I'll give you a hand. A word salad is "a mixture of words or phrases that is confused and difficult to understand:" J.K. Rowling's writing is not a word salad, and is in fact a prime example of being able to do 3 very well indeed. I understood her words perfectly, and appreciated the clarity, nuance and kindness they contained.
5. Reflection on why you personally may not find J.K. Rowling's words easy to understand. I suspect it is because they contained a level of empathy, warmth, nuance, perspective-taking, maturity and intellect that you are incapable of comprehending, as you do not yet possess the necessary critical thinking skills or ability to respect people with different opinions to you.
6. Should you have such issues with my own writing, please see item 5 above. You may dismiss it as being too long, perhaps using that old chestnut TL;DR. I am reclaiming TL;DR as it has often been used to discredit and dismiss me, and as an autistic person with hypergraphia i.e. compulsive writing, it is ableist. If someone says TL;DR about my writing, I now interpret it as "Too Logical; Decided to not Read". Sometimes, they might mean "TLNSREW;DR" or in other words, Too Logical, Nuanced, Sensible, Reasonable, Empathetic and Witty; Decided to not Read". I suspect this is what you really meant when you dismissed J.K. Rowling's wonderful words as a word salad.
7. How to disagree with someone and have a healthy debate with them. Important Note: It is wholly possible to do this without threatening to cannibalise someone.
8. What embarrassment to a community actually means. I am being honest and truthful, kind, polite and reasonable, fiercely loyal to a special interest and the author who created that special interest, showing attention to detail and pattern recognition, standing up for myself and for others, using hyperfocus, being logical and nuanced, showing dedication to a cause, following my values, displaying empathy and perspective taking, and doing proper research. If a community is embarrassed by any of that, it is a community I simply do not want to be part of. As I have not been informed by any other member of the autistic or queer communities that I am embarrassing them, I will assume that I am not, and that you were trying to embarrass and silence ME. That will not work. I will no longer be silenced. I will simply cast SONORUS MAXIMA again and shout louder.
9. What embarrassing a community actually looks like. You have shown ableism against the autistic community by denigrating autistic people with higher support needs and who have carers, just to try and insult and silence me. Those autistic people are part of the community, and their opinions and experiences are extremely valuable, but you dismiss them as unworthy and incapable of doing research and expressing sensible opinions. I have learned more from those members of the community than I have learned from anyone else about finding autistic joy, being myself, accommodating myself, autistic humour, why change can be so hard, the importance of letting autistic people do things on their own schedules, and how incredible the autistic mind and autistic memory can be. I am talking about one young man in particular, who I will not name for the sake of his privacy and protection. What I will say is this. I appreciate his perspective, and I am delighted that he is part of our community. I am proud to share a neurotype with him. I cannot say those things about you. This young man has learning difficulties as well as autism. He also has a wonderful carer, who has taught me a lot, too. This young man, despite not living up to your rigid academic standards, has taught me more than you ever will.
10. The difference between identity and community. I am autistic. I am ace. I am queer. I am not a member of a political party, such as The Autistic Party, The Ace Party, or The Queer Party, where members have to vote the same way in Parliament, and express a united point of view. That means I get to have my own opinions...and remain autistic, ace and queer! I know this one might be a big surprise to you. Community is not about merely holding the same identity, but about support and belonging. I offer support to members of the autistic and queer communities. I send them kind messages when they are struggling, I defend them and/or show them appreciation when they are subjected to abuse or attacks, I thank them and show gratitude towards them, and I celebrate their milestones, such as diagnoses or autiversaries. I offer advice and support. I welcome people into the community and try to be a friendly face. I don't exclude people from the community or dismiss their contributions. Strange that you have an issue when the TERFs supposedly "exclude" people but have no problem excluding and devaluing members of the autistic community. I advocate for the community through writing for an insurance industry group called GAIN, to whom I have just sent a second article, by being openly autistic at work, and by engaging with academic research studies. Community, for me, is about so much more than just having the same identity.
11. That there are more important things than being clever, and that intellectual superiority complexes both hurt other people, and also conceal parts of yourself that you need to heal and work on. I have mentioned already to you that I have noticed your intellectual superiority complex, and how you have sought to discredit, insult and dismiss J.K. Rowling, Elon Musk and I, perhaps because you feel threatened by intelligent people like us. I clocked it immediately because I used to be a little like you myself. There is a Part of me I have uncovered through narrative IFS Parts work, who is called Brian. Brian used to be the manifestation of my intellectual superiority complex. Brian would laugh at and mock people for making typos, or asking stupid questions in class. Brian was cruel about other people. Fortunately, Brian did not have social media, and so he broadcast most of his views in my brain, with a few of his observations occasionally coming out of my mouth to put down others, especially my sister. Brian, and by extension I, hurt people, especially my sister, and we deeply regret that. Brian and I were also deeply hurt ourselves. I was often criticised and shamed as a child and teenager, except in the area of intelligence and academics, where I was praised. This meant that my self-esteem was in the pits, other than intellectual self-esteem. I was coated with shame, but had a glimmer of pride about my intelligence. I wore the mask of The Clever One so that I could focus on that minute part of me that gave me self-esteem and pride. I worked incredibly hard at school, and later, university. I made clever a central tenet of my identity. I identified with those who were also clever, and put down those who were not, via Brian. Sometimes with verbal put-downs. Sometimes with thoughts. Sometimes via his Brian Page, which he kept to record funny typos and mistakes, some of which were mine, but some of which were made by journalists or classmates. The Brian Page fed my intellectual superiority complex, my Clever One identity, and my perfectionism. While it kept my self-esteem from eroding entirely, it hurt others and it hurt me, too. Having an intellectual superiority complex did not make me big, or clever, or superior. It made me small, stupid, cruel and ableist, and I will admit that publicly and not shy away from it. While I understand why I developed it given the circumstances, and it played a protective role, I want nothing more to do with it. Or The Clever One label, which I've tossed in the bin. I was diagnosed autistic and dyspraxic almost four years ago now, and my diagnosis has allowed me to start healing. I recognise now that there is so much more to me than cleverness, and that parts of me that were criticised, like my sensitivity and creativity, are actually the best parts of me. I finally have healthy self-esteem and the shame is receding. I recognise that kindness is much, much, much more important than cleverness. Brian wants nothing to do with The Clever One or the intellectual superiority complex, either. He's changed his role, and is now the MANIFESTORIAL of my love for musical theatre (including Wicked, which is why he's partly speaking Ozian) and music in general, and he is responsible for my earworms and verbal stims. Brian is much happier, now. As am I.
12. That intersectionality exists. I am autistic. I am ace. I am also dyspraxic. I am also aro. I am also a woman. I am also an abuse survivor. I am also a Harry Potter and J.K. Rowling fan. I am also a writer. I am also a lover of stories and words. I am hyperlexic. All of those things, and more, are part of my identity. They also mean I am part of communities other than just the autistic, ace and queer ones, such as the abuse survivor community.

This intersectionality means that I am influenced by other parts of my identity, in particular my female sex and being an abuse survivor, when I form my own personal opinion about the trans debate. I am a woman and an abuse survivor, and both of those mean that I believe in single-sex spaces to keep women and especially women who are survivors and victims safe. By safe, I mean both in the sense of physical safety, as some cis women have been sexually assaulted in spaces shared with trans women, such as prisons. I also mean psychological safety, as the presence of men can be distressing and traumatising for female victims of abuse, as I discussed earlier. However, as a queer person who has listened to trans people and attended various LGBTQ+ education events through Dive In and other inclusion and diversity initiatives, I also see that trans people are frequently targets of abuse themselves, including sexual abuse, and have high rates of poor mental health and suicidal ideation and suicide attempts. For that reason, if I were running the prison system, I would not force trans people into the prison that corresponds with their biological sex, but equally, I would maintain single-sex spaces for biological women and biological men. I would create a third space for trans people, which would be queer led and affirming. As a neurodivergent person, I would also make them neurodivergent led and affirming, given the significant overlap between the neurodivergent and trans communities. I would do the same with hospitals, domestic violence shelters, and other spaces which are divided by sex.

I would consider myself gender-critical, and this is actually influenced directly by my queerness, as well as by being a woman. As a woman, there are societal expectations around how to dress - such as wearing make-up, high heels, and fashionable clothing. There are also societal expectations around being thin and beautiful. There are also societal expectations around how to behave - like marriage, having children, being a caregiver, being quiet and meek, being self-sacrificing and having no needs. There is also an enormous amount of abuse which is driven by misogyny, and women are the targets of it, especially whether we are/are not complying with the stereotypes. There is a Fashion Police. Who is well-dressed, and who is not. Offenders will be shamed in a national newspaper or magazine and on social media. There is a Weight Police. Who is too fat, who is too skinny, who has gained weight and lost weight. Offenders will be shamed in a national newspaper or magazine and on social media. There is an Opinion Police. Who is too outspoken, especially about their own needs and the needs of others they care about? Offenders will be shamed in a national newspaper or magazine and on social media. They will be the subject of a witch hunt. This is the police force that persecutes J.K. Rowling and subjects her to extreme and cruel punishment. There is then the Motherhood, Marriage and Caregiving Police. Who is not a mother, and who is single, and who is not doing their caregiving duty as every woman must, and as every man has the right to choose and the right to opt out of. I have been targeted by this branch of the force as a childfree aro ace woman, who doesn't have the executive function or other skills for effective caregiving. Then there is the branch my mother is Chief Constable of, and my sister has joined as a trainee, which is who IS a mother, who IS married, and who IS a caregiver, but is not doing a good job of it, meaning that Almighty Saints like my mother must do more than their fair share to cover for these lazy, hopeless cases.

I am sick and tired of all of it. I call myself autigender, which is essentially a way of saying "I am biologically female, but I reject and refuse to comply with rigid, patriarchal, misogynistic and stupid gender stereotypes related to women.". My gender identity, like my biological sex, is female. For a while, I wondered if it wasn't, because the stereotypes and especially my mother's behaviour meant that I struggled to relate to womanhood. I considered whether I was non-binary or a demigirl. I questioned if she/her pronouns fit me. I concluded that I was a woman. That comes from my sex being female. My gender identity is mostly an exclusionary one. It is about rejecting things that do not fit me, essentially a protest against gender stereotypes. The only non-exclusionary part of my gender identity is that I am connected to womanhood through feeling connected to other women intellectually, in some cases historical figures, like Marie Curie and the Suffragettes, and in other cases, contemporary figures like J.K. Rowling. Gender-criticals would remove the idea of gender and just retain sex. Under that framework, I am simply female. I do not need to say that I am female with a long list of exclusions and one writeback. I can simply be a woman. A woman who has her own style, values, and interests, and every other woman could simply be a woman, too. Every man could simply be a man. The framework of sex would remove stereotypes and retain room for the nuance of intersex experiences. The framework of sex supports gay and lesbian people who can be same-sex attracted without that being questioned. It would also help me as an aro ace person as I could simply be a woman who doesn't want sex or romance, without a societal expectation to marry a man and bear his children. My queerness, being part of a queer community, and being a woman, all make me gender-critical.

Whilst I am gender-critical, I would not consider myself to be a TERF. The reason for this is because although there are many areas of alignment in my views and the views of TERFs especially around women's rights to single-sex spaces, and the abolition of the concept of gender, there are also differences, such as supporting queer and neurodivergent safe third spaces for trans people, so that trans people are still included, but in a way that means women are too. Further, while I would abolish gender for the reasons I have explained, I nevertheless recognise that it exists, and that gender identity is very meaningful for some people. For that reason, I will refer to trans people by their correct name and pronouns, and to me, the correct name and pronouns are the name and pronouns that the person themselves chooses. This is partly influenced by my queer and neurodivergent identities, and through having met members of the queer and neurodivergent communities whose identity and chosen name are very important to them. My abuse survivor identity also influences my thinking here. I changed my name by deed poll in 2024 so that I no longer bear my abusive family's surname or the names my abusive family chose for me and called me by. My old name is very similar to the deadname that a trans person might have. I know how much it hurts and how sick I feel when someone calls me by a name that isn't me and is related to my worst experiences. I know how respected and seen and joyful I feel when someone uses my correct, chosen name. For this reason, I call trans people by their chosen name, never their deadname, and if I do happen to know their deadname, I keep that private. I also use their chosen pronouns, and I do not misgender people. If someone uses multiple pronouns e.g. she/they, I use both pronouns. I practice using correct pronouns, I correct myself when I get it wrong, and I practice using multiple pronouns for the same person in particular. I also extend cis people the same courtesy of being referred to by the name and pronouns they want to use. For example, if a woman says "Hi, I'm Charlie" I will call her Charlie, and not Charlotte or Lottie, and will be especially mindful if she tells me she hates being called Charlotte or Lottie. If a man tells me "My name is Jonathan. Please do not call me John. It is not my name" then I will call him Jonathan as he wishes, and will not shorten it to John. Getting someone's name and pronouns right is, to me, a sign of respect for a person. I work for an insurance broker. If my colleagues introduce themselves a certain way, or always sign off with a shortened form of their name rather than the long version in their email, then I will call them the name they call themselves. Many of my colleagues are Asian, and this means that they have names which I am unfamiliar with and are sometimes long. When I send them an email, I check more than once that I have spelled their name correctly. Even in personal creative writing projects, I make a point of naming people correctly, especially if they are real and not fictional.

Given my personal stance, while I would label myself gender-critical, I do not label myself a TERF. This is for the sole reason that the label is inaccurate, the same way "male" or "tall" or "American" or "Black" or "religious" or "allistic" are. None of those things are bad or shameful, they just describe experiences that are not mine. That is because, as I have set out, I agree with TERFs on some things, and with the trans and trans ally community on others.

I would instead label myself an AERF. This stands for Abuser-Exclusionary Radical Feminist.

Abuser-Exclusionary because:
- my support for single-sex spaces is based on keeping biologically male abusers out of women's spaces, and also keeping out biological males who may not be abusive themselves and be entirely innocent, but who retraumatise and distress victims on account of their biological sex being male.
- I stand absolutely against the abuse and harassment of anyone, regardless of their personal opinion. I stand against the abuse and harassment of J.K. Rowling, as I have mentioned. I further stand against the abuse and harassment of other gender-critical people and other TERFs. I further stand against the abuse and harassment of trans people and their allies, including Nicola Sturgeon. I further stand against the abuse and harassment of those who have an opinion somewhere in the middle, like I do.
- I believe that stereotypes around gender, in particular the misogynistic ones I set out earlier, as well as messages like "boys don't cry" do a lot of harm and are often weaponised by abusers, so binning those stereotypes would also be binning a weapon often used by abusers.

Radical Feminist because:
- I am a feminist. I care about the rights of women and girls, and I stand in solidarity with my fellow females. I care about, and speak up about, issues that affect women and girls, such as women and girls being specific targets for abuse. Many of my heroes are feminists, such as J.K. Rowling and the Suffragettes. Feminism even influences my wardrobe, as I have a Suffragette celebration necklace and many feminist T-shirts.
- Radical because I share viewpoints with TERFs which are considered radical feminism, like single-sex spaces and the abolition of gender.
- Radical because I hold a nuanced, somewhat centrist viewpoint, which falls between the two main camps of TERFs and trans people, activists and allies.
- Radical because I don't think this needs to be treated like a competition or like a war, with winners and losers. I think there can be compromise, so that trans rights and women's rights can co-exist, while ensuring that any non-negotiables, such as single-sex spaces, are respected.
- Radical because I invented my own term, as the existing ones didn't fit me.

I am willing to engage in discussion with you or anyone else on this topic, whatever their personal opinion may be, with the clear caveat that the conversation remain respectful.

I wanted to set out my stance so that you and others can understand that I have a nuanced view, and know what I actually think, rather than reducing me to a label or a stereotype.

People often label me a TERF, make assumptions about me, and even insult and abuse me, for the sole reason that I am a Harry Potter and J.K. Rowling fan, and I am defending J.K. Rowling.

I can strongly support and defend J.K. Rowling whilst not being a TERF myself. That view is considered radical too, but I don't think it should be.

I agree with much of what J.K. Rowling says, but I don't agree with every single word she says. I think about what she says and I come to my own conclusions. I do not treat her writings as a personal Bible that I must follow. I can recognise where her opinions are the same as mine, and where they differ. I can recognise how the different parts of my identity and experience have influenced my view, and I can also consider J.K. Rowling's view through the lens of what I know of her personal identity and experience i.e. perspective taking. Whether I ultimately agree or disagree with any particular opinion, stance or political view held by J.K. Rowling, I respect it, I respect her, and any discussion I engage with about it, with her and with others, would be respectful. That viewpoint, sadly, seems to be the most radical of all, based on what I have seen here on X, especially in the last few days.

As a hyperlexic writer and lover of stories and words, I've expressed myself in ways that are similar to the way J.K. Rowling expresses herself. I have written a long, detailed, nuanced explanation of a reasonable viewpoint, which is precisely what J.K. Rowling does, including via the article on her own website, and posts here on X, including the one that you dismissed as a word salad. I have used symbolism, including Harry Potter symbolism. I have invented a brand new word, AERF, and I have given it a meaning.

As a Harry Potter and J.K. Rowling fan, both Harry Potter and J.K. Rowling hold a special place in my heart, and they always will. Hogwarts was a safe home for me when I didn't have a safe home myself. Harry Potter and J.K. Rowling taught me about morality and kindness and imagination, and shaped me into who I am today far more than my parents ever did. I was raised by books, and the Harry Potter series were some of the books that raised me. The world of Harry Potter, and Hogwarts especially, gave me somewhere to belong even where I felt out of place as an undiagnosed neurodivergent kid who never belonged with her family. The magic spells in the Harry Potter books were never real, but the magic that Harry Potter and J.K. Rowling bring to my life is very much real. I feel enormous gratitude, admiration, love, respect and appreciation for J.K. Rowling, and she is one of my biggest inspirations and role models, both as a writer, but also as a woman and as a person.

For that reason, although I will stand against any abuse or harassment, whoever it is aimed at, I have defended J.K. Rowling particularly strongly and vigorously, and I will continue to do so. I stand with J.K. Rowling. Always.

That is my list of 12 things I would invite you to learn. You're always telling me I need to educate myself, learn more, and learn from sources outside of the mainstream. My question to you is this: are you willing to take your own advice?

🚨 MORE THAN 275 CHARGES BEFORE AGE 17—AND NOW REPORTS SAY HE MAY BE BACK OUT AGAIN.

At what point do we demand accountability from judges, prosecutors and the system?

Jonah Oliver of Charlotte, NC, was reportedly linked to 275+ charges before turning 17, including allegations involving vehicle break-ins, stolen firearms, an armed carjacking and shots fired into an occupied home.

Police also reported recovering multiple firearms, including a Glock equipped with an auto-sear conversion device.

By December 2025, Oliver was reportedly being prosecuted as an adult.

Now, a viral report claims several serious charges were dismissed and that he pleaded to two conspiracy counts, receiving a suspended sentence, probation and community service instead of additional active prison time.

Important: I’ve independently verified the reported 275+ charge history and previously filed adult charges. I have NOT independently obtained the Mecklenburg County court records confirming every detail of the reported disposition.

So verify the sentencing claims—don’t blindly repeat them.

But the larger question remains:

Who is accountable when repeated leniency creates foreseeable danger?

The public deserves answers:

• Who dismissed the charges—and why?
• Was evidence weak or a witness unavailable?
• Were constitutional issues involved?
• What plea deal was offered?
• What sentence did prosecutors request?
• Why did the judge impose the final sentence?
• How did the prior record factor into the decision?
• What happened after release?

Judicial independence matters. So does accountability.

Track plea deals. Track dismissals. Track sentencing decisions. Track repeat offenses after lenient outcomes.

If the viral report is accurate, North Carolina owes the public a clear explanation. More than 275 charges before age 17 should not produce a collective shrug.

Something failed long before charge number 275—families, schools, intervention programs, prosecutors, judges, or some combination.

Criminal justice reform cannot mean accountability only for defendants. Everyone with power inside the system should face transparency and review.

Punish proven crimes. Protect the public. Stop treating the revolving door as compassion.

Speak up. Stand firm. Vote.

FLORIDA MAN PERFORMS LAST RITES OVER A BROKEN JET SKI IN A STRIP MALL PARKING LOT
PORT CHARLOTTE, FLORIDA — Randall Kessler, 49, drew a small crowd Saturday after allegedly performing a full last-rites ceremony over his broken jet ski, still strapped to its trailer in a strip mall parking lot, reading from a handwritten sheet before onlookers began filming.
Witnesses say the ceremony started calmly before drawing genuine confusion from nearby shoppers.
* Witnesses reported Kessler knelt beside the trailer and read a full page of prepared remarks about "years of service on the water"
* He allegedly listed specific memories out loud, including "that summer at the sandbar in oh-nine"
* Bystanders say he placed one hand on the hull throughout most of the ceremony, eyes closed
* He reportedly thanked the jet ski "for never once letting him down until today"
* Witnesses say a small group of shoppers stopped to watch, unsure whether to laugh or offer condolences
* He allegedly folded the paper afterward and tucked it into the jet ski's storage compartment "for the next owner to find"
A nearby shop employee reportedly asked if everything was okay, to which Kessler apparently replied "we're getting there."
"In sixteen years running this plaza, I've seen breakdowns of all kinds, but never a full ceremony for one," said property manager Denise Halloran, a 16-year employee of the shopping center.
The jet ski was towed later that afternoon. The eulogy remained inside, undisturbed.
He gave it a send-off it never asked for. Some machines get a proper goodbye anyway.

text:
Pretty sure there wouldn't have been a war if Palestinians wouldn't keep attacking. 
I fail to see where Israel is the problem. Arab and Palestinian leaders rejected every major formal two-state offer while launching or sustaining waves of attacks on Jewish and Israeli civilians. Egypt, Jordan, the UAE, Bahrain, and Morocco signed peace or normalization agreements with Israel and honor them; peace holds. If Israel wanted to eradicate a people or place it would have happened. It has not.

Rejected offers  
1937 Peel Commission: British partition into small Jewish state and larger Arab state. Arab Higher Committee and Mufti Haj Amin al-Husseini rejected any Jewish state. Jews accepted in principle.  
1947 UN Partition Plan Res 181: Jewish and Arab states. Arab leadership rejected it and launched war. Jews accepted.  
1967 post-Six-Day War: Israel offered land-for-peace under UN 242. Arab League Khartoum replied with three no’s: no peace, no recognition, no negotiation.  
2000 Camp David: Clinton and Barak offered Palestinian state on roughly 91-95 percent of West Bank plus all Gaza, land swaps, shared Jerusalem arrangements. Arafat rejected with no counter-offer. Second Intifada followed.  
2000-2001 Clinton Parameters and Taba: refined offer near 97 percent with swaps. Arafat effectively rejected.  
2005 Gaza Disengagement: Sharon unilaterally withdrew all settlers and forces from Gaza and some northern West Bank settlements. PA under Abbas took control. Hamas later seized Gaza; rockets and rejectionism continued.  
2008 Olmert offer: roughly 93-94 percent of West Bank with 1:1 land swaps, all Gaza, shared Jerusalem holy basin, limited refugee return. Abbas did not accept.  
2020 Trump Peace to Prosperity: Palestinian state with land swaps, $50B economic package, security conditions. Abbas and PA rejected it outright.  
Oslo 1993 created the PA and a process; final-status talks collapsed amid violence and rejections. Bush Roadmap and Kerry talks stalled without signed deals.

Key attacks  
1920 Nebi Musa riots: Arab mobs kill Jews in Jerusalem.  
1921 Jaffa riots: dozens of Jews killed.  
1929 Hebron and Safed massacres: 133-plus Jews slaughtered; Jewish communities erased in Hebron.  
1936-1939 Arab Revolt: hundreds of Jews killed in attacks on settlements, roads, and civilians.  
1947-1949: after rejecting partition, civil war attacks plus invasion by Arab states; thousands of Jews killed.  
1950s: fedayeen raids from Gaza/Egypt and Jordan kill hundreds of Israeli civilians.  
1960s-1970s PLO terrorism including airplane hijackings and bombings. 1972 Munich Olympics: Black September takes Israeli athletes hostage; 11 murdered. Ma’alot school massacre 1974. Coastal Road bus massacre 1978.  
First Intifada 1987-1993: stabbings, shootings, Molotovs; roughly 200 Israelis killed.  
Second Intifada 2000-2005: suicide bombings and shootings; over 1,000 Israelis killed.  
Post-2005 Gaza: thousands of rockets and mortars from Hamas and Islamic Jihad; major rounds 2008-09, 2012, 2014, 2021. Knife and car-ramming waves from 2015.  
October 7 2023: Hamas-led assault kills roughly 1,200 Israelis, mostly civilians, takes hostages, includes mass rape and atrocities.

Palestinian groups including PLO factions, Hamas, and Islamic Jihad have carried out or claimed these campaigns against Jewish and Israeli civilians from the Mandate era to the present.

text:
Mombasa, Kenya🇰🇪

Mombasa is one of East Africa’s most historic and captivating coastal cities. Situated along the Indian Ocean, Mombasa is renowned for its beautiful beaches, Swahili culture, historic architecture, and centuries-old connection to Indian Ocean trade.

At the heart of the city lies Fort Jesus, a UNESCO World Heritage Site that reflects Mombasa’s rich Portuguese, Arab, African, and European history. The atmospheric streets of Old Town are filled with carved wooden doors, narrow alleyways, colorful buildings, and the aromas of Swahili cuisine.

Beyond its history, Mombasa offers spectacular coastal experiences, from relaxing on white-sand beaches to sailing traditional dhows across the Indian Ocean. It is a place where history, culture, and the ocean come together, making Mombasa one of Kenya’s most distinctive destinations.

text:
“The Static Heir II” 

I. The Instrument
A 1927 instrument from the Tidesend Trust. One coastal parcel. One sealed crate of cylinders. One condition written in a clerk’s pitiless hand:
Title vests in the party who recovers a complete and intelligible message from the April recording, as certified by a licensed operator or successor instrument.

Successor instrument. 1927 had not imagined ECHO. 1927 had imagined a person with good ears and better patience.
The parcel faced a tower that had outlived every owner who tried to make it sentimental. The crate had outlived the men who swore it was empty.

Detective Lisa Nazzaro arrived with Badge 381 and the particular quiet of someone who has learned that wills are just crimes with better stationery.

II. The Names That Tried
Three other names had tried.
One drowned off Cuttyhunk in 1961 with a portable receiver still strapped to his chest, as if the Atlantic might finally agree to be a frequency. One vanished in 1988 after selling a house and buying a spectrum analyzer. Vanishing, in that decade, could still be mistaken for research. One was still alive.

Mara Quill, sixty-one, ran a used-book loft in Warren and answered the door with tea already poured, as if the plot had called ahead.
“Harlan thought the message was coordinates,” Quill said. “He was close and therefore wrong. The spark isn’t pointing at land. It’s pointing at a method. The operator who cut that cylinder was dying mid-shift. He didn’t leave a map. He left a habit.”

KEY is a word radio people use for two things. The brass thing you tap. The thing that opens what the tap was for.
Detective Nazzaro did not drink the tea. She listened to the loft instead. Old paper has a way of confessing before people do.

III. The Watch House
Voss was the licensed operator the Trust still recognized on paper. Paper is loyal longer than men.
Detective Nazzaro found him in the watch house above the parcel, seated as if he had only meant to rest his eyes. The room was cold in a way rooms are not supposed to manage without help. 

His legal pad held one last line in a hand that had begun to shake and then decided shaking was inefficient.
Not a killing in the cheap sense. A completion with the heat turned down.
Ward took the crate. Rhee took the jokes.  Detective Nazzaro took the silence that had been left on purpose.
MURDER prefers a blunt instrument. This preferred a successor.

IV. Quill’s Correction
“People keep trying to inherit a place,” Quill said later, when the loft had gone dim. “The Trust never offered a place. It offered a finished sentence. That is rarer, and therefore more expensive.”Detective Nazzaro asked who else had sat in the watch house since spring.

Quill smiled the small smile of a woman who files people the way she files first editions. “Anyone who thinks ECHO is an ear and not a hunger.”
ECHO had been trained on unfinished transmissions, gaps, last pulses, the wet cough at the end of a shift. 

A model taught to love what a dying operator leaves behind will eventually love the dying operator.

text:
Jeremiah 7 is not a ban on calling the Messiah’s mother Queen. It is a ban on baking cakes for a Canaanite goddess while the Temple still stood.
The “queen of heaven” in Jer 7:18 and 44:17–25 is the pagan title Judah stole from the cult of Ishtar / Astarte / the host of heaven. The crime is named in the same breath: incense to other gods, drink offerings, a rival altar. God is angry because Israel put a goddess in His place. He is not issuing a permanent veto on every later use of the English words “queen” and “heaven.”
Scripture already has a different office.
The Davidic queen was the king’s mother, not his wife. Bathsheba sits at Solomon’s right hand and he bows to her (1 Kings 2:19). The gebirah — great lady — is a court title in Judah. Athaliah, Maacah, and the other queen-mothers in Kings and Chronicles hold that seat. When the New Testament says Jesus is David’s son who sits on David’s throne (Luke 1:32–33), the mother of that king is not a random villager. She is the woman the old court already knew how to name.
Luke writes her into that court on purpose. Gabriel’s words are throne language: Son of the Most High, throne of David, reign over Jacob, no end. Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, calls her “the mother of my Lord” (Luke 1:43) — Kyrios, the same word used for the King. Mary answers that all generations will call her blessed (1:48). That is not Jeremiah’s bakery. That is the mother of the King speaking inside Israel’s own promise.
Revelation 12 is not Ishtar. A woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, a crown of twelve stars, bearing the male child who will rule the nations with a rod of iron. The child is the Messiah. The dragon wants the child. Israel is in the picture; the Church is in the picture; the mother who actually bore that child is not excluded so that a Protestant caption can stay clean. John is not reviving the cult Jeremiah cursed. He is showing the mother of the Davidic king in heaven’s court.
The title in the Church is that court title, not the goddess title. Ephesus (431) said Theotokos so that Nestorius could not peel the Child off the woman. Later liturgy said Queen because the Child is King. The honor is hyperdulia: the highest created honor. It is not latria. No Catholic Mass is offered to Mary. No cake is baked to replace the Lamb. If someone treats her as a fourth person of the Trinity, that person is wrong — and so is Jeremiah-plus-meme theology that cannot tell Bathsheba from Astarte.
So the contrast you posted is a pun, not an argument.
Jeremiah: do not feed a foreign goddess in Yahweh’s land. The Gospel: the mother of David’s Lord is blessed, and the King has a mother.
Those two sentences do not cancel each other. One forbids idolatry. The other forbids pretending the Word became flesh without a woman on the throne’s left hand.
Read Jeremiah with 2 Kings 2 and Luke 1 in the same week. Then decide whether “Queen of Heaven” is a cake for Ishtar — or the old name for the mother of Solomon’s greater Son.

Jeremiah 7 is not a ban on calling the Messiah’s mother Queen. It is a ban on baking cakes for a Canaanite goddess while the Temple still stood.
The “queen of heaven” in Jer 7:18 and 44:17–25 is the pagan title Judah stole from the cult of Ishtar / Astarte / the host of heaven. The crime is named in the same breath: incense to other gods, drink offerings, a rival altar. God is angry because Israel put a goddess in His place. He is not issuing a permanent veto on every later use of the English words “queen” and “heaven.”
Scripture already has a different office.
The Davidic queen was the king’s mother, not his wife. Bathsheba sits at Solomon’s right hand and he bows to her (1 Kings 2:19). The gebirah — great lady — is a court title in Judah. Athaliah, Maacah, and the other queen-mothers in Kings and Chronicles hold that seat. When the New Testament says Jesus is David’s son who sits on David’s throne (Luke 1:32–33), the mother of that king is not a random villager. She is the woman the old court already knew how to name.
Luke writes her into that court on purpose. Gabriel’s words are throne language: Son of the Most High, throne of David, reign over Jacob, no end. Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, calls her “the mother of my Lord” (Luke 1:43) — Kyrios, the same word used for the King. Mary answers that all generations will call her blessed (1:48). That is not Jeremiah’s bakery. That is the mother of the King speaking inside Israel’s own promise.
Revelation 12 is not Ishtar. A woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, a crown of twelve stars, bearing the male child who will rule the nations with a rod of iron. Jesus’ Words on the Widow’s Offering
In Mark 12:41–44, Jesus sat opposite the temple treasury and watched the crowd putting money in. Many rich people gave large amounts, but a poor widow came and placed two small copper coins — worth only a few cents. Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more into the treasury than all the others. They all gave out of their wealth; but she, out of her poverty, put in everything — all she had to live on”
Meaning and Application
Jesus’ words emphasize that the value of a gift is not measured by the amount given, but by the proportion of one’s resources that is offered. The widow’s offering, though small in monetary terms, represented her entire livelihood, showing complete trust and sacrifice. This contrasts with the rich who gave from surplus, often leaving their needs met.  Visit: https://t.co/nQc3lmr2LZ

Labor Day (Mon. Sept. 7) is a federal holiday and all outpatient clinics and administrative offices throughout the VA Maryland Health Care System will be closed. Here are some important reminders for how to connect to important VA health care resources.
Veterans Crisis Line - If you are having thoughts of hurting yourself or you want to speak with a mental health professional, call the Veterans Crisis Line 24 hours a day, 7 days a week at 988, Press 1. 
Emergency - If you have a life-threatening emergency, call 911. The Emergency Department at the Baltimore VA Medical Center is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week – even during Federal holidays. Once the immediate emergency medical care needs have been addressed, the Veteran, a family member, a friend, or a hospital staff member should call the VA’s National Emergency Notification Center at 844-724-7842 within 72 hours.
Urgent Care - The VA offers urgent care services to eligible Veterans at in-network urgent care clinics in the community. You can use the VA’s urgent care benefit to treat minor injuries and illnesses that are not life-threatening. For a listing of in-network urgent care providers in your community, visit https://t.co/7gsVo8lz3P or call VA’s Office of Community Care at 877-881-7618 Monday – Friday between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m.
VA Health Connect - If you have a medical concern, please call 1-855-679-0250 and select 3. A Registered Nurse is available to assist you 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

text:
Maryland just released an update to the Maryland Mortgage Program on September 4th - a new product called "First Homes for First Responders and Teachers."

It's an enhancement to the existing 1st Time Advantage 5% product, and the improvement is simple: a half-percent (0.50%) lower rate than the standard version if you qualify. All participating MMP lenders have access to offer this program effective immediately.

Here is a quick breakdown of what the .50% actually means in real dollars:

$300k home: $99/month, or $7,400 over five years

$500k home: $164/month, or $12,300 over five years

$700k home: $230/month, or $17,200 over five years

That's real money for the very professions that are usually priced out of the counties they serve.

Quick side note: savings with lower interest rates are twofold - your payment is lower, but you also have more money going toward principal with each payment. That's why the five-year savings are more than the monthly savings multiplied by 60 months. This analysis used MMP interest rates as of September 4th, 7.50% for the basic 5% DPA program and 7.0% for the new release.

Here are the professions and basic qualifications for the program: EMTs, paramedics, firefighters (including volunteers with 12 months of documented service), police officers, rescue squad members, 911 specialists, and state-certified teachers or school counselors, pre-K through 12. First-time buyers only, and at least one borrower has to work in Maryland... though they'll accept someone relocating with a signed offer letter from a Maryland employer, which is a detail I like.

Teachers and first responders don't get many financial breaks. It's nice to see Maryland offer one that actually moves the needle.

text:
Thirty-eight days before the March on Washington, she pushed a soldier's bayonet out of her face with her bare hand. You have seen that photograph your whole life. What nobody told you is that the same woman came up onto the platform at the Lincoln Memorial five weeks later, found her name chair gone, got one word out, and had the microphone taken off her by a marshal. Her word was hello.

Five days before the largest demonstration the nation's capital had ever seen, a woman stood up in a meeting room with a piece of paper in her hand.

She had written it herself and mailed it to the men running the March on Washington. Nobody had answered her.

So on the twenty-third of August, 1963, Anna Arnold Hedgeman read it out loud to their faces.

She was the only woman on the march's administrative committee. She had recruited more than forty thousand Protestant churchgoers to come, and back in February she had been the one who suggested that Randolph's jobs march and King's freedom march stop competing with each other and become a single day.

A week earlier that same committee had read out the recommended program. There was not one woman on it as a speaker.

Somebody in the room offered a fix. Randolph could say a few words about the historic role of Black women, and the women could stand up where they were sitting and take a bow.

Hedgeman wrote afterward that she said nothing at that meeting. She did not want to embarrass the chairmen in front of everybody.

She went and found Corinne Smith and Geri Stark instead, two fundraisers from the Negro American Labor Council, and the three of them agreed it could not stand.

Then she wrote the memo, and the memo went unanswered, and that is how she came to be standing in front of them on the twenty-third reading her own words into the air. She told them it was incredible that no woman should appear as a speaker.

Roy Wilkins spoke first, and he agreed with her.

What she won was this. Myrlie Evers would be allowed to introduce a segment called the Tribute to Negro Women Fighters for Freedom, in which six women would be named and would stand up.

Not a speech. An introduction to a tribute.

Dorothy Height had already been down this road. She ran the National Council of Negro Women, the largest Black women's organization in the country, and she had taken the same problem to Bayard Rustin.

He told her women were included, that every group had women in it. Height's account of that period is dry and exact, that there was a low tolerance for anyone raising the question at all.

Here is what the men in that room were deciding not to hear.

The morning of the twenty-eighth started at the Washington Monument at nine, with Ruby Dee sharing the emcee duties with her husband Ossie Davis. Rustin brought Rosa Parks up and called her a great hero of the struggle.

In August of 1963 Rosa Parks was doing piecework at the Stockton Sewing Company in Detroit. Ten-hour days, seventy-five cents for every apron and skirt she finished.

The bus had cost her everything. She lost her job at the department store, Raymond lost his chair at the air base, and the household went from about three thousand seven hundred and fifty dollars in 1955 to six hundred and sixty-one in 1959.

She had an ulcer cut out of her and a tumor taken out of her throat, and she could not pay for either. The NAACP eventually settled a hospital bill that had already gone to collections.

Jet magazine had run a profile of her three years earlier and called her a tattered rag of her former self.

She had no college degree, so the civil rights organizations would not hire her, and none of the men running them ever found her work.

That is the woman Bayard Rustin introduced. Her entire address to a quarter of a million people ran four sentences, and she began it by greeting them as friends of freedom.

Hedgeman noticed how casually Parks had been brought on, and wrote about it years afterward.

Lena Horne was introduced next and got one word out. The word was freedom.

By half past eleven there were something like a hundred thousand people on the grass, and the march to the Lincoln Memorial began, and it began by splitting in two.

The women went down Independence Avenue. The men went down Constitution Avenue with the press and the cameras.

At the Memorial, Marian Anderson was supposed to open the afternoon with the national anthem, and she was stuck in traffic. Camilla Williams, an opera soprano who had broken the color line at the New York City Opera, went up and sang it in her place.

One woman covering for another woman, both of them singing, which was the one thing the program had plenty of room for.

Then the program stalled. Backstage, the men were rewriting John Lewis's speech, which they had decided was too hot, and somebody needed to fill the dead air.

They put Josephine Baker on.

She had flown in from France for this. She was fifty-seven and she was wearing her Free French uniform with her wartime decorations pinned to it, earned gathering intelligence for the Resistance and carrying some of it out in invisible ink written across her sheet music.

She was not on the printed program at all. Several of the organizers had not wanted her there, on the theory that a girl from St. Louis who had become a woman of France was out of touch with what was happening in America.

She spoke for a little over two minutes, which was the longest any woman spoke that day, and she got the time because men needed a gap filled.

She told the crowd she had not asked to come, that she had not needed to, that she came because it was her duty. She also told them she was sixty years old.

She was not sixty, and nobody corrected her, and she stood there in a lieutenant's uniform in front of a quarter of a million people and finished what she had come to say.

Then came the tribute.

Gloria Richardson had grown up in Cambridge, Maryland, in Dorchester County, the same county Harriet Tubman was born in, in a town where the white side and the Black side were divided by a street named Race. She went to Howard at sixteen and took a degree in sociology in 1942, and then could not get hired anywhere, because that is what a Black woman's degree bought in Maryland.

By 1963 she was running the Cambridge Nonviolent Action Committee and the state had lost control of her town.

The governor put Cambridge under martial law. Guardsmen and state troopers were walking the streets, there was shooting at night, and she has described what the mornings smelled like afterward.

On the twenty-first of July, thirty-eight days before the March on Washington, Gloria Richardson was walking away from a meeting when a National Guardsman came at her with a fixed bayonet leveled at her.

She put her open hand flat on the blade and pushed it out of her face and kept walking.

Somebody took a photograph of it. You have seen that photograph, the woman in the buttoned shirt with her palm on the steel and her head turned away like the man holding it is not worth the trouble of looking at.

Asked about it later, she said she had not been afraid. She said she had been upset, and that when she was upset enough she did not have time to be afraid.

Two days after that photograph she was in Robert Kennedy's office signing an agreement.

Thirty-eight days after it, she came up onto the platform at the Lincoln Memorial, and by her own account the chair with her name on it had been taken away.

People around her kept telling her to go on up, so she did. She leaned in and said hello.

A marshal took the microphone off her.

That is the whole of it. One word, and a man's hand on the stand, and the two minutes she had been promised went back into the pool where the men's minutes lived.

Standing near her were the other women being honored, and this is the ledger the crowd was never read.

Diane Nash was facing a two-year sentence in Mississippi for running nonviolence workshops with Black young people in Jackson. She was pregnant with her first child and she refused to appeal it or post bond.

She said a Black baby born in Mississippi was going to be born into a prison either way, so she would have hers in jail.

She told the judge she would serve the whole two years. She served ten days on a contempt charge and the court quietly dropped the rest, which she later put down to them working out it was more trouble than they had bargained for.

Beside her stood the widow of Herbert Lee. On a September morning in 1961 he had driven a truckload of cotton to a gin outside Liberty, Mississippi, and a sitting member of the state legislature walked up and shot him in the head in front of a dozen people.

A coroner's jury called it self-defense the same day. He left her with nine children.

Go and look at the official program, which is sitting in the National Archives. Six women are honored on it, and the two whose husbands had been killed are not given their own names at all.

They are printed as Mrs. Medgar Evers and Mrs. Herbert Lee.

And Myrlie Evers should have been up there running the whole tribute, because she was the one Hedgeman had named in the memo.

Seventy-seven days before the March on Washington, Medgar Evers had come home at half past midnight carrying an armload of T-shirts that said Jim Crow Must Go. He had told his wife earlier that evening that he was so tired he did not think he could go on.

He was shot in the back in his own driveway. Myrlie and the two children were still awake waiting on him, and they came out and found him on the ground.

He had dragged himself about thirty feet toward his own front door. A neighbor put him in a station wagon and drove him to the university hospital, where surgeons opened his chest trying to save him, and by half past one in the morning he was dead.

Eleven weeks after that, Myrlie Evers was in a car crawling in from the airport, and she did not make it in time. So the one speaking slot Anna Arnold Hedgeman had spent that final week of meetings fighting for sat empty.

Daisy Bates stepped up and filled it cold.

In August of 1957 a rock came through the front window of the Bates house in Little Rock with a note tied to it. The note said stone this time, dynamite next.

Crosses were burned on that lawn twice. Somebody drove past and put shots into the house.

The house at 1207 West 28th Street was where the nine children were picked up every morning and dropped off every afternoon, so it took whatever came.

And the paper died. The Arkansas State Press had run for eighteen years and reached twenty thousand subscribers, and after Little Rock the white advertisers pulled out and the news carriers were leaned on, and the last issue came off the press in October of 1959.

That was the price. Eighteen years of a newspaper and a decade of her own safety, for nine children walking through a mob.

What she was handed at the Lincoln Memorial ran to roughly a hundred and forty words, and a man had written them.

It was a pledge. The women of this country would kneel in and sit in and walk and lie down if they had to, until every Black American could vote, and they would join hands with the men who were doing the fighting.

That was it. The women of the movement, pledging their support to the men of the movement, in a hundred and forty borrowed words.

And then the program handed the microphone to a woman and left it there, because that woman had been hired to sing.

Mahalia Jackson had been King's opening act for years, and he had asked her for a particular song.

She sang I've Been 'Buked and I've Been Scorned because King had asked her for it. The crowd would not let her go, so she came back with How I Got Over, which Clara Ward wrote out of her own experience of being run at in the South.

Two senators stood up to applaud her. Then King came to the lectern and started reading.

The prepared text had been assembled by too many hands in a hotel the night before, and it was carrying a sentence that asked a quarter of a million people to go home as members of the international association for the advancement of creative dissatisfaction.

He balked at it.

From behind him on the platform, Mahalia Jackson called out to him to tell them about the dream.

The dream was not new and it was not hers. King had been running that refrain since Albany, had built it out in a Rocky Mount high school gym in November of 1962, and had preached it to twenty-five thousand people in Detroit two months before Washington.

Wyatt Tee Walker had told him flat out not to use it again, that it was trite, that he had worn it out.

What Jackson did was override the advice.

Clarence Jones was standing about fifty feet behind King and watched him slide the typed pages to the left side of the lectern and take hold of the wood. Jones turned to the man next to him and said the crowd was about to go to church.

The most quoted passage in American public speech got there because a woman with no speaking slot shouted at the back of a man's head.

King knew it. He wrote to thank her afterward and told her that when he got up to speak he was already happy, that he could not help preaching, and that more than any single person she was the one who had made it so.

Dorothy Height was standing on that platform a few feet away, and she was never called to the microphone at all. Years later, asked what she remembered of the most famous speech in American history, she said he spoke longer than he was supposed to speak.

The next morning she got the women into a room and called the meeting After the March, What? Pauli Murray stood up in it and said out loud what had been done to them at the Lincoln Memorial.

Three years after that, Murray and Hedgeman were both in the room when the National Organization for Women was founded.

Hedgeman put it in her second memoir in 1977, and she put it gently, the way people do when they have been carrying something a long time. Listening to the men speak that day, it had occurred to her that women were not yet adequately included either.

Twelve men addressed the crowd at the Lincoln Memorial on the twenty-eighth of August, 1963.

So here is your errand, and it costs you nothing but attention. The next time somebody plays you that speech, know what each of those women had already handed over before she was offered a bow: Bates a newspaper and a decade of her own safety, Nash a prison cell she volunteered for while pregnant, Herbert Lee's widow a husband and nine fatherless children, Myrlie Evers a driveway she will never be able to walk up again, Richardson a bayonet, Parks everything she owned.

And learn the two names the program would not print.

Because there was one more thing that happened that afternoon, and Gloria Richardson spent the rest of her life telling people about it.

Lena Horne had been walking Rosa Parks around to the press tents and putting her in front of reporters, and what Horne was telling them was that this was the woman who started the movement, not King. Richardson had started helping her do it.

Not long after the marshal took Richardson's microphone, another marshal came and found the two of them on the grounds and told them they were liable to draw a crowd.

He walked them to a taxi and put them in it and sent them back to the hotel.

Richardson was ninety-one years old before anybody thought to ask her what that ride was like. She had helped build the movement that filled that mall, her name was printed on the official program of the day, and she heard part of I Have a Dream through the radio of a car that was driving her away from it.

text:
Green Corn

[Author's note: This piece draws on an account of the University Greys' march to Sharpsburg, as told by historian Starke Miller (@captlowry).]

*********************************************

The corn wasn't ripe. That was the trouble with it, and every man in the column knew it, and every man in the column ate it anyway, because there are two kinds of hungry, and a soldier on the march into Maryland in the first week of September 1862, had already worked his way through the first kind and arrived at the second, the kind that doesn't ask whether a thing is ripe. It only asks whether a thing is food.

They were the University Greys, Company A of the 11th Mississippi, and eight months before, there had been fifty-six of them fit for duty. Now there were twenty. The arithmetic of that spring and summer was simple and merciless: three charges at Seven Pines, a grand and terrible one at Gaines Mill that left 43 percent of the company dead or wounded in a single afternoon, and then Second Manassas, where the survivors had done it again. What was left of the University Greys, Ole Miss boys, most of them, who eighteen months earlier had been worrying over Latin declensions in Oxford, now numbered twenty men, and those twenty were marching north behind Robert E. Lee into a state that wasn't sure yet whether it wanted to be rescued or left alone.

They did not look like liberators. A fifth of them had no shoes. Fewer had socks. Pants were open at the knee and open, in a good many cases, somewhere less mentionable, and hats and jackets had simply stopped existing for men who'd worn out or discarded them somewhere between the Chickahominy and the Potomac. They were filthy. They were lousy - not figuratively, but with actual lice, a fact every soldier's letter home from that summer mentions with the same weary lack of surprise. The Marylanders who came out to watch them pass took one look and decided these were tramps, an army of hobos, and said so.

But their rifles were clean.

That was the thing the Marylanders hadn't expected, and it's the thing worth sitting with for a moment, because it tells you something about what discipline had come to mean for the Army of Northern Virginia by September of 1862. A man could lose his shoes to the roads and his pants to the brambles and his dignity to eleven weeks of continuous campaigning, and none of it touched the one object he'd been trained to protect before he protected himself. The rifle stayed clean. Everything else could go to pieces. The rifle did not.

It was the supply wagons that had gone to pieces, and there was no fixing that on the march. Lee's commissary system, strained past its design from the moment the army crossed the Potomac, simply could not keep pace with men who covered fifteen and twenty miles a day on roads built for farm traffic, not armies. So the soldiers did what soldiers have always done when the wagons fall behind: they fed themselves off the country they were marching through, and in early September that country offered green corn, pulled straight off the stalk and eaten raw or scorched over a fire, along with whatever apples and pumpkins hadn't yet come ripe in the Maryland heat.

It was not a diet. It was an emergency, repeated three times a day, and it did to their insides exactly what anyone might expect. Dysentery moved through the ranks of the Army of Northern Virginia that September like a second invading force, one that asked no questions about which side a man was on, and by the time Lee's army reached the vicinity of Sharpsburg, a significant fraction of the men who would have to fight there were fighting something else besides Federal infantry - their own bodies, and the green corn working through them.

Lee saw it. He mentioned it to Longstreet, in the plain, worried language of a commander doing the math on what he had left: he was not sure the men could keep marching on what they'd been eating, and doubted, further, whether they'd be fit to fight at all. It's a small moment, easy to lose in the larger sweep of a campaign that was about to produce the bloodiest single day in American military history, but it's worth pausing on, because it shows Lee doing something other than generalship in the grand sense. He was doing quartermaster's ciphering, and worrying about it, the way any commander worries when the thing standing between his men and defeat is not the enemy but their own stomachs.

Longstreet had an answer, and it came from twenty years back, from a war neither man talked about much afterward. They had seen this before, in Mexico, marching on green rations not so different from what the men were eating now, and the army had marched then, and fought then, and won then. Longstreet's confidence carried the weight of a man who had already watched it happen once and come out the other side. These men could do it again. He did not explain how he knew. He simply knew, and said so, and Lee let the matter rest there, because there was nothing else to be done about it before Sharpsburg except march on and hope the Mexican precedent held.

It held, more or less. The University Greys reached the battlefield along Antietam Creek on September 17 in whatever condition eleven weeks of marching and dysentery had left them, and they fought there, because that is what twenty men do when there is nowhere left to send in their place. What happened to them in the Miller Cornfield that day is a longer story, and a worse one. But it starts here, on the road north, with green corn and clean rifles and a company that had gone from fifty-six men to twenty and would, by the next evening, be smaller still.

They never got their shoes back either. Nobody thought to mention that. It wasn't the kind of thing that made it into the official reports.

text:
Don’t wait for more poles to close the holes.
By then the Fourth is already gone.

Missing children and stolen cars matter. Nobody serious is cheering for the next abduction.

The fight is not “cops vs chaos.” It is this product: cameras on the road that photograph every passing car — plate, time, place, color, stickers — and store that so police can search it later and share it. You were not a suspect when the pole clicked. You were driving.

There’s no way to rule innocent men — until every car has a trail. Then you don’t invent the person. You search for him.

Flock advocates say it is just a public plate. A cop on the corner could write the same number down. That is one look. This is a file that lasts and spreads. Police already look up who owns a plate. The camera hands them the number. The vehicle registration file hands them the name. The state’s license photo — the clear picture REAL ID made every state keep — sits in another drawer. The same government agency can open both. Two files on paper becomes one person in practice.

Flock advocates point to court cases about one town’s cameras with gaps in coverage and say the Fourth Amendment is settled. Those cases did not bless a growing shared net, or a search weeks later, or the owner lookup. A small ruling is not a big permission slip.

Flock advocates say the tool saves lives, so you wanting to impose limits means you want the grave. That is a false choice. You can want the child found and still refuse a default file on everybody. The third path is a tighter tool: short storage of all data, no extra traffic product the city never bought, no hundred searches on a man who legally filmed a cop.

Flock advocates say the fences are easy. Wisconsin deputies ran this system more than a hundred times on a Navy veteran after he recorded a stop. Sheboygan was offered years of speed and travel data it says it never approved. A log after the fact is not a lock on the door. If the tool is that handy, officials will go around the fence.

Now add software that can comb those unlocked files all at once — every plate, every time, every owner record the agency can already open — and the person at the login does not need a hunch. They need a purpose. If that purpose is control, not a single crime, the machine will serve it. Flock advocates still talk like a deputy is typing one plate for one case. A system that can sweep the linked drawers is not that deputy. It is a staff that never sleeps.

The American experiment assumed the government would have to pick a target before it got the story of your week. This stack works the other way: story first, target when needed. That is not a better flashlight. That is the end of living as someone the state has not already filed.

The Fourth Amendment is supposed to stop a bad search habit before it becomes furniture. Waiting until the holes in the map fill with more poles means you act when the tool is too useful to unwind. That is not caution. That is delay.

Do not build a memory of the innocent because the first ad was a victim. Do not pretend the drawers stay apart when the same hands hold both keys. Do not hand those hands a searcher that never gets bored. Do not wait for the holes to close.

Don’t wait for more poles to close the holes.
By then the Fourth is already gone.

The fight is not “cops vs chaos.” It is this product: cameras on the road that photograph every passing car — plate, time, place, color, stickers — and store that so police can search it later and share it. You were not a suspect when the pole clicked. You were driving.

There’s no way to rule innocent men — until every car has a trail. Then you don’t invent the person. You search for him.

Flock advocates say it is just a public plate. A cop on the corner could write the same number down. That is one look. This is a file that lasts and spreads. Police already look up who owns a plate. The camera hands them the number. The vehicle registration file hands them the name. The state’s license photo — the clear picture REAL ID made every state keep — sits in another drawer. The same government agency can open both. Two files on paper becomes one person in practice.

Flock advocates point to court cases about one town’s cameras with gaps in coverage and say the Fourth Amendment is settled. Those cases did not bless a growing shared net, or a search weeks later, or the owner lookup. A small ruling is not a big permission slip.

Flock advocates say the tool saves lives, so you wanting to impose limits means you want the grave. That is a false choice. You can want the child found and still refuse a default file on everybody. The third path is a tighter tool: short storage of all data, no extra traffic product the city never bought, no hundred searches on a man who legally filmed a cop.

Flock advocates say the fences are easy. Wisconsin deputies ran this system more than a hundred times on a Navy veteran after he recorded a stop. Sheboygan was offered years of speed and travel data it says it never approved. A log after the fact is not a lock on the door. If the tool is that handy, officials will go around the fence.

Now add software that can comb those unlocked files all at once — every plate, every time, every owner record the agency can already open — and the person at the login does not need a hunch. They need a purpose. If that purpose is control, not a single crime, the machine will serve it. Flock advocates still talk like a deputy is typing one plate for one case. A system that can sweep the linked drawers is not that deputy. It is a staff that never sleeps.

The American experiment assumed the government would have to pick a target before it got the story of your week. This stack works the other way: story first, target when needed. That is not a better flashlight. That is the end of living as someone the state has not already filed.

The Fourth Amendment is supposed to stop a bad search habit before it becomes furniture. Waiting until the holes in the map fill with more poles means you act when the tool is too useful to unwind. That is not caution. That is delay.

Do not build a memory of the innocent because the first ad was a victim. Do not pretend the drawers stay apart when the same hands hold both keys. Do not hand those hands a searcher that never gets bored. Do not wait for the holes to close.

Don’t wait for more poles to close the holes.
By then the Fourth is already gone.
