text:
Gentile believers. Paul was not merely irritated by a denominational difference. He saw the finished work of Christ being robbed in broad daylight by men carrying Bibles.

1. A Work of Grace Had Only Recently Begun in Galatia

The word “soon” in Galatians 1:6 is not decorative. Paul was astonished by the speed of the Galatians’ movement away from the truth. They had not been walking in the gospel for several generations and slowly accumulated layers of religious tradition. The work among them was still fresh. In the Galatian region Paul had preached a message that directly contrasted justification in Christ with justification by the law of Moses: “And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses” (Acts 13:39). That statement contains the seed of the entire Galatian controversy. Paul preached that believing sinners were justified by Jesus Christ from the very things from which Moses could not justify them. The law could name their crimes, expose their guilt, pronounce the sentence, and shut their mouths, but it could not clear the guilty. Christ could. Paul and Barnabas preached through persecution, opposition, and physical danger; disciples were made; believers were confirmed; and elders were ordained in the churches. Then, before the dust had settled on the road behind the apostles, religious contractors arrived to remodel the foundation. They did not bring a hammer to the pagan temple. They brought a chisel to the gospel.

Paul’s astonishment becomes sharper when we notice that he says they were “removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ.” Their departure concerned more than a theological diagram. To move from grace to law was to move from the God who had called them. False doctrine is never merely an intellectual rearrangement when it strikes the gospel. A man cannot change the ground of justification without changing his relationship to the One who justifies. The Galatians may have imagined that they were adding greater holiness, deeper roots, ancient authority, and biblical discipline to their faith. Paul told them that they were being transferred away from the grace of Christ. Religion called it advancement; Paul called it removal. Their new instructors probably congratulated them for progressing beyond Paul’s elementary message into a fuller obedience. Paul answered that they were not climbing to a higher floor; they were abandoning the building. Grace does not need the law to strengthen it, any more than the sun needs a candle nailed beside it to improve the daylight. Once human performance becomes a condition of justification, grace has not been enhanced. It has been evacuated.

The historical circumstances make their quick defection understandable without making it excusable. These were churches in a world where Jewish synagogues, pagan temples, Roman customs, family pressures, and traveling teachers all competed for authority. Paul’s apostolic preaching had disrupted the old order, and the cross offended both self-righteous religion and Gentile philosophy. A message declaring that sinners were justified freely through Christ left no room for Jews to boast in circumcision or Gentiles to boast in wisdom. Once Paul departed, teachers with a more respectable-looking arrangement could offer the Galatians something the flesh always enjoys: a visible system by which men can measure themselves against other men. Grace leaves the sinner empty-handed before God; law religion gives him a ruler, a calendar, a ceremony, and something to display. The Galatians were attracted to a system that looked stricter while being spiritually lower. They were leaving the liberty of sons for the bookkeeping of servants. Paul marveled because they had seen Christ presented among them, received the Spirit by faith, and tasted the liberty of grace, yet they were already reaching for the chains from which the gospel had delivered them.

A SECOND CHANCE ON A QUARTER-CENTURY-OLD DOOR: CAN NIGERIA MAXIMISE AGOA'S EXTENSION TO 2028?
On 1 September 2026, the US House of Representatives voted 370 to 48 to extend the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) through 31 December 2028, mirroring a Senate vote passed weeks earlier. The measure, folded into a short-term Continuing Resolution funding the US government, now awaits the President's signature. For Nigeria and 31 other sub-Saharan African beneficiary countries, the extension removes an immediate cliff-edge: AGOA had already lapsed once, on 30 September 2025, throwing exporters into months of uncertainty before Congress restored it retroactively. The renewal buys time. Whether Nigeria uses that time to finally build a non-oil export industry to the United States, rather than simply breathing a sigh of relief, is now the only question that matters.

AGOA has been in force for a quarter of a century. Congress created it in 2000 to give eligible sub-Saharan African countries duty-free access to the US market for more than 1,800 product lines, provided they meet governance criteria — progress toward a market-based economy, the rule of law, political pluralism and due process. Countries that fall short can be stripped of eligibility, as Gabon, Niger, the Central African Republic and Uganda were in January 2024. The programme has never offered reciprocal access to African markets in return, which is precisely why American manufacturers have periodically questioned its value, and why its renewal has grown more contested with each cycle: an initial push for a three-year extension in January 2026 stalled, before the current two-year compromise emerged attached to a funding bill, with no substantive reform of a programme that US business groups themselves describe as designed for a goods-centric economy that increasingly overlooks services and digital trade.

text:
#OnThisDay September 6, 1912: Prairie Insurgency.

Theodore Roosevelt brought his Progressive Party presidential campaign to Fargo during a western railroad tour. Speaking from the rear platform of his campaign train and later before a larger gathering, the former president sought votes and strengthened the organization of a new political party. His appearance placed Fargo within one of the most consequential presidential contests in American history. The election divided the Republican Party, expanded the national debate over governmental responsibility, and demonstrated that a third-party candidate could challenge the established political system.

Roosevelt entered the campaign after failing to wrest the Republican nomination from President William Howard Taft. Roosevelt’s supporters accused party leaders of controlling the Republican National Convention and denying their candidate legitimately elected delegates. In August 1912, they organized the Progressive Party and nominated Roosevelt for president, with California governor Hiram Johnson as his running mate. Popularly called the Bull Moose Party, the new organization competed against Taft, Democrat Woodrow Wilson, Socialist Eugene V. Debs, and Prohibition nominee Eugene W. Chafin.

North Dakota offered fertile ground for insurgent politics. Its farmers faced railroad charges, grain-marketing disputes, corporate concentration, and dependence upon distant financial centers. Political reformers had already challenged established Republican leadership. In the March 1912 Republican presidential primary, Wisconsin senator Robert M. La Follette defeated Roosevelt in North Dakota, while Taft finished a distant third. Roosevelt therefore arrived in Fargo neither as the unquestioned leader of state progressivism nor as the nominee of its dominant party. He needed to transfer reform-minded voters from La Follette’s movement into the new Progressive organization.

Contemporary motion-picture footage establishes the character of Roosevelt’s Fargo campaign. The surviving film shows men, women, and children surrounding the train while Roosevelt leans across its railing to address them. Other sequences show him speaking from a decorated platform before a large assembly. Additional scenes depict Native men, women, and children gathered on the open plains as Roosevelt speaks from the train. George E. Roosevelt, the candidate’s cousin and campaign secretary, also appears. Photographs preserved by the Institute for Regional Studies record the campaign train at Fargo’s Great Northern depot.

The train served as both transportation and political stage. Railroad campaigning enabled Roosevelt to reach dispersed western communities, conduct brief appearances, and generate local newspaper coverage. Fargo’s status as a railroad center made it a logical campaign destination. The city connected agricultural North Dakota with Minneapolis–Saint Paul, the Great Lakes, and eastern commodity markets. Roosevelt’s presence also linked national reform proposals with the economic concerns of farmers and commercial communities throughout the northern plains.

The Progressive platform supplied the political substance behind the spectacle. It endorsed direct presidential primaries, direct election of United States senators, initiative, referendum, recall, women’s suffrage, campaign-finance disclosure, regulation of lobbying, and stronger public control over interstate corporations. Its labor program called for restrictions on child labor, occupational safety standards, workers’ compensation, minimum wages for women, and limits on working hours. The platform also supported federal supervision of problems that individual states could not manage effectively. These proposals presented government as an instrument capable of restraining concentrated power and protecting public welfare.

Roosevelt’s Fargo visit held special meaning because of his established association with North Dakota. He had hunted and ranched in the Little Missouri Badlands during the 1880s. In a 1910 Fargo speech, he declared that his North Dakota experiences had helped prepare him for the presidency. His 1912 return allowed the Progressive campaign to use that personal connection while constructing a formal state organization around his candidacy.

The November results showed both the strength and limits of Roosevelt’s appeal. Wilson carried North Dakota’s five electoral votes. Roosevelt nevertheless finished second nationally and became the principal opponent recorded in the Electoral College tally, receiving 88 electoral votes to Wilson’s 435 and Taft’s eight. No subsequent third-party presidential candidate has equaled Roosevelt’s electoral-vote total.

The Fargo appearance remains historically valuable because it survives in photographs and motion-picture film. These records document the physical form of early twentieth-century campaigning: the railroad car as podium, the depot as political forum, and the gathered crowd as both audience and visual evidence of popular politics. Roosevelt did not carry North Dakota, but his September 6 campaign revealed the state’s place within the Republican revolt of 1912 and the national movement to enlarge democratic participation, regulate economic power, and expand governmental responsibility.

🙄 I think a lot of the assignment of importance to this theory is based on the post hoc fallacy.  This "pervasive propaganda" model (my own shorthand for what the tweet mentions) seems to be a blueprint for what Trump thought would work for him, and so far all he's done has made people hate him.

How about a real-world example...   South Africa.  😆 😆😆 

Before the Boers and English showed up, there were a few different Bantu-speaking ethnicities, the most populous being Zulu and Xhosa.  I checked a few books I have here in the house tonight and they mentioned gold having been found in more ancient cultures' graves, for example the Venda's ancestors who were invaded by "Hottentots" (an old derisive word probably referring to "bush men" or "San," but it wasn't a precise term).  The seizure of land from native peoples was based on the usual colonial attitude that any non-white, less technologically advanced culture is inferior to white Europeans.

Then, to jump to the part Americans are more familiar with... Boers and English show up... Boer War (1899-1902) .. gold and diamonds brought in prospectors from California, Australia, and other countries... Apartheid (1948-1994).  

Apartheid separated the black and white populations, but in effect was a brutal form of racial repression.  What I'd consider to be a civil war went on for about 30 years before it ended.  While the US had moved on from slavery and was working on wiping out its remaining segregation, South Africa refused to change its race-based system.  And so, while the US government refused to offer more than verbiage encouraging the change, American people took what action they could.

I don't think that apartheid was very stable to start, although I wasn't born at the time it started, and so I'll quote a book I had on my shelves, "The Boer War" by Denis Judd and Keith Surridge, p. 301 (one of the last pages of the book, because the book was on the Boer War and not apartheid -- just something quickly found on my shelves):  "The system of Apartheid ultimately failed not simply because of its essential inhumanity, or because of the belated economic pressure brought to bear on the regime by the United States and other Western powers.  What fatally undermined it was the ideology at its core -- its lack of inclusiveness, though of  course this also carried a moral dimension.  While blacks, Indians and coloureds remained outside the privileged structure, no whites could ever really feel that their long-term future was guaranteed or that they could sleep safely in their beds."

I remember the last decade of apartheid, and I don't necessarily agree with that quote -- it seemed that the violent civil war could have continued for another 30 years without apartheid falling.  Western countries, including the US, were sick of hearing about police in South Africa beating black kids to death every day.  It was in our news like Vietnam had been, night after night.

It wasn't just the white South Africans keeping it in effect, though.  I had a book in college (which may or may not be in storage somewhere) talking about transnational corporations in South Africa.  I know that IBM sold systems to track its population for the apartheid regime.  Coca-cola was pressured to withdraw from the country, among others.  

There was a college divestiture movement, where protesters demanded that their colleges divest from companies doing business in South Africa.  Students at University of Wisconsin took over a building and eventually won a resolution to divest in 1978.  In 1986, Harvard students were demanding the same from its Board of Overseers.  (Old article linked below.)  This was economic pressure applied to the transnational corporations, to encourage them to leave South Africa.  Meanwhile, some celebrities refused to perform in South Africa.

This was international pressure to shame South Africans and make their lives more difficult as encouragement to change their system, and hopefully people's attitudes.  Eventually under Reagan, in 1986 the US passed sanctions on South Africa at a time of economic vulnerability, and this caused transnational corporations to leave the country, while lowering the standard of living.  Eventually the government was reformed, and Nelson Mandela was elected.

There are a few relevant issues here -- 1.) The revolution was already in place, after people were removed from their native lands.  It wasn't encouraged through a propaganda campaign in schools, the press, and so on, and was eventually successful.  2.) The offending attitudes didn't come from radical teachers -- they came from the ruling class' pursuit of natural minerals, their belief of superiority, their family traditions, and life experience.   3.) The government didn't start a propaganda campaign, rather it was an obstacle to change.  4.) Ultimately outside influences changed their culture through international ostracization and imposed financial hardship.

In essence, life doesn't follow the theory, at least not in all cases.  "Leftists" was an irrelevant label in this case.  This was an indigenous population rejecting its mistreatment at the hands of their invaders' descendents.

During Joan's youth, a prophecy circulating in the French countryside, based on the visions of Marie Robine of Avignon, promised an armed virgin would come forth to save France.[56] Another prophecy, attributed to Merlin, stated that a virgin carrying a banner would put an end to France's suffering.[57] Joan implied she was this promised maiden, reminding the people around her that there was a saying that France would be destroyed by a woman but would be restored by a virgin.[58][d] In May 1428,[61] she asked her uncle to take her to the nearby town of Vaucouleurs, where she petitioned the garrison commander, Robert de Baudricourt, for an armed escort to the Armagnac court at Chinon. Baudricourt harshly refused and sent her home.[62] In July, Domrémy was raided by Burgundian forces[63] which set fire to the town, destroyed the crops, and forced Joan, her family and the other townspeople to flee.[64] She returned to Vaucouleurs in January 1429. Her petition was refused again,[65] but by this time she had gained the support of two of Baudricourt's soldiers, Jean de Metz and Bertrand de Poulengy.[66] Meanwhile, she was summoned to Nancy under safe conduct by Charles II, Duke of Lorraine, who had heard about Joan during her stay at Vaucouleurs. The duke was ill and thought she might have supernatural powers that could cure him. She offered no cures, but reprimanded him for living with his mistress.[67]

text:
As a Dutchman, Spain occupies a strange and wonderful place in our history.

We fought an Eighty Years' War against the Spanish Crown, built part of our national identity around that struggle, and still teach names like William of Orange, Philip II and the Duke of Alba in school. You would think that might make Spain the historical villain in the Dutch family story.

Instead, I feel an enormous affection for the country.

Spain is one of Europe's great civilisations. Romans and Visigoths, centuries of Islamic rule, the Christian kingdoms and the Reconquista all left their marks there. Then came the Spain of Columbus, Magellan's expedition, conquistadors and an empire that connected Europe with the Americas and Asia on an extraordinary scale.

Spanish influence is still visible across much of the world. Hundreds of millions speak the language. Cities thousands of kilometres from Madrid carry Spanish names. Spanish architecture, religion, law, food and customs crossed oceans and became woven into entirely new cultures.

And then there is Spain itself.

Old plazas that come alive in the evening. Churches and cathedrals standing where generations before us worshipped. Families taking their time over food. Tiny bars where several plates somehow become dinner. Football treated with the seriousness of a minor religion, local festivals that can involve anything from solemn processions to people being chased through streets, and villages that still seem intensely proud of being that particular village.

I admire that.

The Dutch and Spanish have a particularly interesting relationship because our histories are tied together through both conflict and exchange. The Habsburg Netherlands were ruled by the same monarchy that ruled Spain, and our revolt against Philip II eventually became the long struggle from which the independent Dutch Republic emerged.

There was terrible violence on both sides. Spanish troops sacked cities in the Netherlands, while the Dutch revolt produced its own brutality. Our ancestors weren't especially talented at conducting polite disagreements.

Yet the story didn't end in 1648 when Spain finally recognised Dutch independence.

Over the centuries that followed, Dutch and Spanish merchants continued doing business, diplomats maintained relations and our countries gradually went from old enemies to European neighbours, partners and friends. Today thousands of Dutch people travel south every year, while Spaniards live, work and study here. What was once a relationship shaped by armies and dynasties is now so ordinary that most of us barely think about how remarkable that transformation is.

I also think our differences make the relationship more enjoyable.

The Dutch schedule dinner. The Spanish appear to regard our dinner time as a late lunch.

We like directness, planning and knowing approximately when something will end. Spain has taught generations of Dutch holidaymakers that an evening can simply continue until everybody decides it has finished.

But underneath those differences I recognise something familiar: attachment to family, region, local traditions and a strong sense that culture belongs to the people who inherited it.

That is why I want Spain to remain unmistakably Spanish.

I want Andalucía to feel different from Galicia, Catalonia different from Castilla, and a Spanish town to offer something that could never be recreated perfectly in Amsterdam. Europe becomes poorer when those differences disappear.

Our ancestors spent eighty years fighting over who would rule the Netherlands.

More than four centuries later, I can look south and feel no need to diminish Spain to celebrate Dutch independence. In fact, understanding what a formidable civilisation our ancestors were fighting makes our own history more interesting.

Spain helped shape us partly through friendship, partly through exchange and, admittedly, for quite a long time by trying to prevent us from leaving.

Families can be complicated like that.

But after centuries of shared European history, Spain doesn't feel distant to me.

It feels like one of those relatives with whom we once had an absolutely spectacular argument, eventually made peace, and somehow never stopped being connected.

I’ve been researching changes to our “church meetings.” (Yes, this is what I do for fun.)

Here’s some notable dates/changes (I may be wrong with some of these):

Apr 6 1830 — First sacrament meeting (Tuesday)

Aug 1831 — Sacrament ordinance linked to Sunday (D&C 59)

Apr 1836 — Weekly Sunday sacrament begins (Kirtland); fast day is the first Thursday of the month

March 17, 1842 — Relief Society organized

1850s — Weekly sacrament meeting becomes standard in Utah

1856 — fast day, first Thursday of the month, adds testimony meeting

Dec 1849 — First Sunday School (for children on Sunday morning)

Nov 1867 — Sunday School organized churchwide for youth

Dec 1867 — every ward to have a Relief Society with meetings twice a month

1870 — Young Ladies’ Retrenchment Association

1875 — Young Men’s Mutual Improvement Association

1876 — Ward sacrament meetings replace citywide meetings

1877 — Sacrament added to Sunday School for children; young ladies renamed YWMIA

Aug 1878 — Primary begins (weekday)

1896 — Fast day (and testimony meeting) moves from first Thursday to first Sunday 

1904 — Adult Sunday School classes offered (Sunday morning)

1908 — Priesthood meeting for men on Monday nights

c. 1908–10 — Young men begin blessing the sacrament

Mar 1912 — Individual sacrament cups replace common cups

1930s — Priesthood meeting moves to Sunday morning

1941 — Nursery offered

1946 — Silence during the sacrament instead of preaching/music

1950 — Only those holding priesthood office to prepare the sacrament table.

Mar 1980 — Three-hour block; Sacrament Meeting/ Sunday School / Primary / Relief Society all in one. All members take the sacrament in one meeting. Youth activity once a week.

Oct 2002 — missionary farewells discontinued

Jan 2019 — Two-hour block

Sept 6 2026 — Second hour split into shorter classes

Manifest Destiny: The widespread belief in the United States that the nation was destined to expand across the North American continent to the Pacific Ocean. 

Annexation of Texas: The U.S. annexed Texas as a state in 1845 after Texas gained independence from Mexico in 1836; Mexico still viewed Texas as its rightful territory. 

Border Dispute: The U.S. claimed the southern border of Texas was the Rio Grande, while Mexico insisted it was further north at the Nueces River. 

Failed Land Purchases: President James K. Polk attempted to purchase California and New Mexico from Mexico, but the Mexican government refused the offer. 

Key Battles: 

Battle of Palo Alto & Resaca de la Palma (May 1846): Early engagements in Texas where General Zachary Taylor defeated Mexican forces after initial border skirmishes. 

Battle of Contreras & Churubusco (August 1847): General Winfield Scott’s forces drove Mexican defenders back during the campaign toward Mexico City. 

Battle of Chapultepec (September 1847): U.S. forces successfully assaulted Chapultepec Castle in Mexico City, famously defended in part by young Mexican military cadets (Los Niños Héroes). 

Outcomes

Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848): The peace treaty that officially ended the war, setting the U.S.-Mexico border at the Rio Grande.

The Mexican Cession: Mexico ceded over 500,000 square miles of territory—about half its total landmass—to the United States, including modern-day California, Nevada, Utah, New Mexico, and parts of Arizona, Colorado, Wyoming, and Kansas.

Financial Compensation: The United States paid Mexico $15 million and assumed certain damage claims.

Sectional Tensions: The vast new territory reignited fierce debates in the U.S. over the expansion of slavery, ultimately laying groundwork for the American Civil War.

text:
**Lioness Season 3: Joe Thought She Was Hunting Russian Spies—Until She Became the Target**

*Lioness* (also known as *Special Ops: Lioness*) is Taylor Sheridan’s tense Paramount+ spy thriller that follows a secret CIA program using female operatives—called Lionesses—to infiltrate terrorist and hostile networks from the inside. The series stars Zoe Saldaña as Joe McNamara, a seasoned CIA senior case officer who runs the unit while trying to keep her family life from collapsing under the weight of her classified work. By Season 3, which began streaming in August 2026, the show shifts its focus from Middle Eastern terrorism to the Russia-Ukraine war and a sprawling Russian intelligence operation on American soil.

Joe is no ordinary case officer. She previously served as a Lioness operative herself and carries the psychological scars of high-risk missions, including one that led to the death of a major terrorist leader. She is tough, morally conflicted, and constantly balancing operational ruthlessness with the need to protect her husband Neal and their children. In Season 3 she is pulled into unfamiliar territory when a Ukrainian intelligence officer named Oleksandra Balakin—played by Elizaveta Neretin—approaches the CIA with extraordinary information.

Oleksandra is a long-term mole inside Russia’s SVR, the foreign intelligence service. She offers the location of Aleksi Yurimov, a high-value Russian official described as “Putin’s hammer” who runs a special hybrid-warfare unit. The CIA decides the prize is worth the risk. Joe and a small team, including Cruz Manuelos, are inserted into the Donetsk front lines alongside Delta Force operators. They fight through trenches, North Korean soldiers supporting Russian forces, and brutal close-quarters combat to capture Yurimov alive. The extraction succeeds, but it comes at a cost and immediately paints a target on the Lioness team.

Two days after Joe returns home to Virginia, the blowback arrives. Men posing as state police try to force their way into her house. Joe kills them. The attackers turn out to be Belarusian contractors working for Russian intelligence. What began as an identification probe quickly escalates. Later, Joe is abducted in a professional snatch operation. Her captors strip her, search for tracking devices, and make it clear they know exactly who she is. The hunter has become the hunted.

The rest of the season follows the Lioness team as they scramble to find Joe while simultaneously trying to understand how the Russians identified her so quickly. Suspicion immediately falls on Oleksandra. Joe and her colleagues interrogate the Ukrainian agent, accusing her of playing both sides. Oleksandra insists the failed attack on Joe’s home was a Russian probe designed to confirm her identity after the Yurimov capture. She argues that if the SVR had wanted Joe dead or disappeared earlier, they would have succeeded. Reluctantly, the CIA keeps her in play because her access inside Russian intelligence is too valuable to discard.

Oleksandra’s files reveal a much larger problem. Russia has cultivated a network of American assets that includes low-level officials, journalists, a school superintendent, judges, members of Congress, and even two U.S. senators. Some of these people were recruited through classic honeypot operations—the same methods Oleksandra herself used while posing as an SVR officer. The CIA faces an ugly choice: expose the network and risk public panic and institutional collapse, or quietly turn the compromised officials into double agents.

text:
Katherine Johnson's father broke his own household in two for eight years so his daughter could go to high school. Their county in West Virginia would not teach Black children past the lower grades, so every September his wife took four kids a hundred and twenty-five miles across the state to a rented house, and every June they came back, and he stayed behind farming to pay for all of it. He had six years of schooling himself. You know what she went on to do at NASA. You have never once been told what it cost him.

On the eighteenth of September, 2024, five gold medals were set out in Emancipation Hall at the United States Capitol.

Four of them carry a face and a name. One of those four is Katherine Johnson, whose family had to come forward to accept it, because she had been dead for four years by then.

Her medal shows her portrait in front of a spread of orbital equations, and on the back, a chalkboard diagram of the Apollo 11 lander linking up with the command module.

That is a good design. It is the exact piece of work she named, when people asked her, as the thing she was proudest of in thirty-three years.

The fifth medal shows a group of women watching Apollo 11 come down on the Moon.

Not one of them has a face, and that was not a mistake or a cost saving. The United States Mint explains the choice in its own published description of the medal, and the explanation is worth reading slowly.

By placing the women in silhouette, the Mint writes, they appropriately represent any and all of the women to be honored by this medal.

Turn the medal over and there is a constellation on the back, Andromeda. The Mint chose it partly because Andromeda is also called the Chained Woman, and it stands there for the obstacles these women broke through.

The only words on it are HIDDEN FIGURES and ACT OF CONGRESS 2019.

So the country did the one honest thing available to it. Asked to honor the Black and white women who did the mathematics for NACA and NASA from the nineteen thirties to the nineteen seventies, it struck an outline that would fit any of them, because there is no complete list of who they were.

There never was one, and building it is still going on right now.

The law that ordered those five medals was signed on the eighth of November, 2019.

It took five years to get them into that room. Minting takes time, and then a pandemic took more.

Katherine Johnson died on the twenty-fourth of February, 2020, three months and sixteen days after that signature. The congresswoman who introduced the bill, Eddie Bernice Johnson of Texas, died in 2023.

Neither of them was in the room.

Back up seven years from that hall and you find a forty-thousand-square-foot computing building at NASA Langley in Hampton, Virginia, with her name across the front. Back up again and you find a book in 2016, a film that followed it, and a Presidential Medal of Freedom put around her neck in 2015, when she was ninety-seven.

She is, by a wide margin, the most nameable Black woman in the history of American science. Now walk the whole thing backward, because every piece of it runs through one line of type on the cover of a government report, and getting that line took an argument.

Start in April 1970, two hundred thousand miles out.

An oxygen tank on Apollo 13 had ruptured and taken most of a service module with it. The crew had moved into the lunar module to stay alive, and the lunar module was not built to be a lifeboat, and everything aboard that could be switched off had been switched off.

To point a spacecraft you have to know which way you are facing, and the way you know is by finding a star you recognize and taking a sighting on it.

NASA's account of Katherine Johnson's career credits her earlier work on backup procedures and charts with helping set a safe path for that crew's return. She was, in other words, part of the redundancy, the thing you reach for when the machines are gone.

Then the emergency actually arrived, and even the backup had to be improvised around.

The explosion had thrown a cloud of debris out alongside the spacecraft, and the service module was still venting gas. In sunlight, the debris glittered.

NASA's own guidance and navigation analysis of the mission says plainly that the crew could not tell the wreckage from the stars, and that the standard alignment procedures could not be run at all.

So they took their sightings on the Sun, the Moon and the Earth instead, the three things too big to be mistaken for anything else. Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise came home on the seventeenth of April.

You will see a children's book title that says Katherine Johnson saved Apollo 13. That is more than the record supports, and the real version is better.

The return burns were worked by the Mission Planning and Analysis men in Houston. What she had helped build was part of the floor underneath them, the answer to the question of what a crew does when there is nothing left to trust.

Her own line about that whole program is the flattest sentence in her file, and it is the one worth carrying.

Everybody was concerned about them getting there, she said. We were concerned about them getting back.

Nine months earlier she had watched the first Moon landing on a small television with a few other people, having contributed calculations for the parking orbit of the Apollo 11 command and service module.

She said, more than once, that the Apollo work was the part of her career she was proudest of. But it was not the thing that made her famous, so go back eight more years.

In early 1962, NASA was preparing to put John Glenn into orbit, and the orbit had been handed to machines.

A worldwide tracking network had been built for it. IBM computers in Washington, at Cape Canaveral and in Bermuda had been loaded with the equations that would carry Friendship 7 from liftoff to splashdown.

The astronauts did not trust them. The machines hiccupped, and they blacked out, and a hiccup at seventeen thousand miles an hour is not a filing error.

So Glenn, going down his preflight checklist, told the engineers to get the girl to run the numbers by hand.

He meant Katherine Johnson, and he did not use her name. She was in the building and she heard about it.

She had been described that way over a telephone once before, in 1953, and that call had changed her entire life.

Her account of what Glenn said next has been quoted by NASA for years. If she says they are good, then I am ready to go.

She sat down with a mechanical calculating machine and worked the same equations the IBMs had been given, by hand, on paper.

It took her a day and a half. Think about what a day and a half at that desk actually was.

No drama and no music, just a woman in her forties going line by line through the arithmetic that would decide whether a man came out of the sky in one piece, knowing that if she got it wrong nobody would ever be able to tell her so.

The numbers matched. Glenn flew on the twentieth of February and he came home.

Here is where the version passed around online goes wrong, and it matters, because the truth is harder and better.

She did not design the trajectory for that orbital flight. NASA's own photograph caption says what she was known for, which is verifying the calculations the electronic computers had already made.

The trajectory analysis she did with her own hands belonged to Alan Shepard's Freedom 7 the year before, in May 1961, America's first human spaceflight.

And two years before Glenn flew, she had coauthored the NASA report laying out the equations for exactly that kind of flight, an orbital mission that has to come down in a chosen place.

Margot Lee Shetterly, who wrote the definitive account of her, puts it plainly. Those equations formed the basis of the orbital flight Glenn would fly.

So the woman NASA called in to check the machine was the woman who had helped write the mathematics the mission was built on, and not one person in that building thought to say so out loud.

Go back once more, then, to September 1960, and the report itself.

The title is Determination of Azimuth Angle at Burnout for Placing a Satellite Over a Selected Earth Position. It is dense, and it is free to read online, and almost nobody who shares her story has opened it.

She put the last touches on the manuscript on the Friday after Thanksgiving, 1959. Then it went into the editorial machinery for ten months of meetings, analysis, recommendations and revision before it went to print.

She wrote it with an engineer named Ted Skopinski. By every account, including her own, most of the work in it was hers.

When publication came round, that turned into a problem, because no woman in the division had ever had her name on a report.

The section head was a man called Henry Pearson. Johnson said plainly, in her own words, that he was no fan of women.

Skopinski was being moved to another assignment, and Pearson wanted the thing finished and off his desk.

Her account of how it broke is one of the plainest sentences in her whole record. Finally, Ted told him, Katherine should finish the report, she has done most of the work anyway.

So Ted left Pearson with no choice, she said. I finished the report and my name went on it, and that was the first time a woman in our division had her name on something.

Look at what that sentence actually describes.

A Black woman had done most of the work on a piece of research, and it took a male colleague saying so out loud to the section chief before her name would go beside his on the cover.

She was not given it and she did not win it in a hearing. Somebody with standing had to say the obvious thing in a room where it could be heard.

She signed it Katherine G. Johnson.

That surname was about three months old when she finished the manuscript. She had married Jim Johnson in August 1959, and the G in the middle stood for Goble.

Goble was her first husband, and to understand what that initial is doing there you have to go back three more years, to the worst stretch of her life.

James Francis Goble died in December 1956, of a brain tumor.

She was thirty-eight. They had three daughters, Constance, Joylette and Katherine, and they had moved the family to Newport News four years earlier so that she could take a job that had not yet turned into anything.

She was back at her desk at Langley in January, and there was no widow's provision in any of it. She worked, she raised three girls, and colleagues describe her in those years logging the kind of hours that leave no evening in them.

She played bridge at lunch, at her desk, viciously, with two engineers named Al Hamer and John Young.

And most mornings she rode to work with the same woman. Her name was Eunice Smith.

She was Katherine Johnson's neighbor and went to the same church, she was a West Area computer, and by Shetterly's account she was Johnson's best friend at Langley.

The two of them took a week off work every single year to go to a basketball tournament of historically Black colleges.

Hold on to Eunice Smith, she is going to matter at the end of this.

Now go back to 1958, and the argument that made everything downstream possible.

The reports her numbers went into were discussed in editorial meetings, in a room, by the men whose names went on them. She was not in the room.

She asked to be. Her own words, recorded on tape in 2011 and held now by the American Archive of Public Broadcasting, are as flat as a shopping list.

I asked permission to go, she said. And they said, well, the girls do not usually go.

And I said, well, is there a law.

There was not. There were laws in Virginia governing where a Black woman could eat, drink and use a bathroom, and there was no law at all about that meeting.

It was simply how it had always been done, which is an answer that has held more people down than any statute ever written.

Her boss let it go, and she began attending the briefings. The first time she walked into one, a man asked a question about a set of figures, and another man said Katherine is here, ask her, she did it.

That exchange is the entire mechanism of her fame, sitting there in one line.

Nobody promoted her into that room. Nobody discovered her.

She asked whether there was a law, and there was not, and every single thing downstream of that question is the report, the Medal of Freedom, the film, the building in Hampton and the medal her children collected in 2024.

Which leaves the only question this story is actually about. What happened to the women who asked and were told no, or who never got close enough to ask.

She had come to Langley in the summer of 1953, into a section of the laboratory called West Area Computing.

It was the segregated pool, and it existed because Virginia law and federal practice required that Black women doing mathematics for the government do it in a separate building, eat in a separate part of the cafeteria, and use separate facilities. The white women computed on the east side.

NASA still holds the floor plan of the West Area cafeteria from 1944, with the segregated arrangements drawn onto it.

Getting into that building cost them more to begin with. By the Smithsonian's account, Black applicants had to arrive with more qualifications than white ones, including a chemistry course completed at Hampton Institute, and Black computers were paid less than white ones for the same work.

Two weeks after she arrived, the section's supervisor, Dorothy Vaughan, sent her out on loan to the Maneuver Loads Branch of the Flight Research Division.

She never came back. Vaughan stayed.

The section's first two heads had both been white women, and Vaughan was promoted to run it in 1949, which made her the first Black supervisor NACA ever had. She used the job to push for promotions and raises for computers who deserved them, including white ones in other groups.

When West Computing was dissolved in 1958 she did not keep a management position. She sought another one at Langley for the rest of her career and never received it, and she retired in 1971.

Her own words are now cast into the back of her Congressional Gold Medal. I changed what I could, and what I couldn't, I endured.

Eunice Smith stayed too.

The women in that pool did the same arithmetic Katherine Johnson did. They read data off film records from wind tunnel runs, worked it through by hand with slide rules and adding machines, plotted it onto graphs, and handed it to an engineer.

The engineer wrote the report. The engineer's name went on the report.

That was not an oversight or a slight. That was the design of the job.

There was a small cardboard sign on their table at the back of the cafeteria. It said COLORED COMPUTERS.

One of the first women hired into the pool, a chemist named Miriam Mann who was not quite five feet tall, started taking it. She would come in, see it waiting there on the table, lift it off and put it in her purse.

It would be gone a few days, sometimes a week, and then an identical one would turn up in the same place, and she would take that one too. Her husband told her she could lose the job over it and she kept doing it anyway.

At some point during the war the sign went into that purse and never came back, years before Katherine Johnson ever set foot in the building.

The separate office stayed, and the separate bathrooms stayed. And you should know that the most famous scene about those bathrooms did not happen to Katherine Johnson.

The film has her sprinting across the campus for forty minutes at a stretch and a white supervisor swinging a crowbar at the sign for her. In the book it is built on, she says she never went looking for the colored bathroom at all.

Most of the bathrooms were unmarked, because the unmarked ones were understood to be the white ones. She used them.

By the time anybody raised it with her she had been doing it for years, and she simply refused to change, and refused to so much as walk into the other kind, and nobody ever said another word to her about it.

The frustration in that scene was real, but it belonged to Mary Jackson, over on the east side, sent hunting for a bathroom by women who laughed instead of answering.

Hollywood took one woman's humiliation, handed it to a different woman, and then handed the rescue to a white man who did not exist.

Keep going back, because the thing that put her in that building had already cost her thirteen years.

In 1939, the president of West Virginia State College picked her to be one of the first three Black students admitted to the graduate program at West Virginia University. She was the only woman among them.

She lasted one semester and left to get married. Then came thirteen years of teaching in segregated public schools and raising three daughters, with a mathematics training that had been built for her personally sitting unused the entire time.

Her professor at West Virginia State had been W. W. Schieffelin Claytor, the third African American ever to earn a doctorate in mathematics. He had designed a course in analytic geometry for one student, because she had already taken everything else the college offered.

Neither of them knew whether there was anywhere in America she would be allowed to use it.

She was thirty-four when the phone call came about Langley, at a wedding, from a relative. And now go all the way down, to 1928, and a ten-year-old.

Katherine Coleman's father was Joshua McKinley Coleman, born in White Sulphur Springs in 1881. He left school after the sixth grade.

He farmed, cut timber, worked as a handyman and a janitor, and took work at The Greenbrier, the enormous resort hotel that made the town's name, in an era when the guests he served would not have been permitted to sit in a room with him.

Her mother, Joylette, had been a schoolteacher before the children came, and Greenbrier County ran no public school for Black children past the lower grades. The accounts differ on exactly where the wall stood, sixth grade in some, eighth in others, and either way it stood.

The oldest daughter, Margaret, hit it first. Her father sent her a hundred and twenty-five miles across the state to Institute, where there was a Black high school attached to West Virginia State College.

The following year he sent the whole family. He could not find work in the Kanawha Valley, so he did not go with them.

Every September, Joylette Coleman moved into a rented house in Institute with four children. Every June they came back to White Sulphur Springs for the summer.

They did that for eight years. A former schoolteacher took work as a domestic to keep that rented house running, and a man with a sixth-grade education stayed a hundred and twenty-five miles away and farmed, so that his four children could sit in a classroom.

The daughter, Joylette Hylick, put the whole thing in six words. He was hellbent on getting his children educated.

The ten-year-old they were doing it for had been counting since she could talk.

I counted everything, she said. The steps to the road, the steps up to church, the number of dishes and silverware I washed, anything that could be counted.

She went into high school at ten and came out of it at fourteen, and she finished college at eighteen. None of which she could have done in the county where she was born.

So here is the ledger this story leaves you holding.

A man with six years of schooling broke his own household into two for eight years and paid for it with his own labor, so that a girl could learn mathematics that a nation would later hand an astronaut's life to.

The country took the whole return on that, and did not write down the names of the women who worked beside her.

Shetterly, who grew up in Hampton with a father who worked at Langley, has a sentence for this that is worth more than any tribute. Katherine Johnson was exceptional, she says, but she was not an exception.

Her Human Computer Project, run now with Duchess Harris and partnered with the Smithsonian, is still open and still recovering names, and it is nowhere close to done. There are hundreds it has not reached.

Not destroyed in a fire, and not lost. Just never written down, because the job was built so the arithmetic would arrive without a person attached to it.

So here is the errand, and it costs nothing but a phone call.

If your family has a woman in it who worked at Langley, or at Hampton, or at any of those laboratories in the forties and fifties, and all anybody ever said about her was that she was good at figures and worked for the government, that is not a family anecdote. That is a missing line in a list somebody is actively trying to finish, and the project takes submissions.

She is in a photograph on somebody's wall right now with nothing written on the back. Now the counting, for what the record can still give us.

Five women in Langley's first computing pool in 1935. Roughly four hundred women computing there by 1946.

Ten women reassigned by the memo that closed West Computing on the fifth of May, 1958, which sits in the National Archives in Philadelphia under identifier 81215360 and can be read online for free.

One name added to the cover of one report in September 1960.

And four faces cast in gold in 2024, beside a fifth medal on which the faces were deliberately left off, so that it could belong to anyone.

That silhouette is not carelessness. It is the most accurate thing the United States could strike, eighty years late, about work it took and never bothered to sign.

Asked near the end of her life what it had been like to be Black in that workplace, or to be the woman who broke the rule about the meeting room, Katherine Johnson mostly gave people the same answer. I was just doing my job.

She rode to work most mornings with a friend who was doing the same job for the same country in the same years, and who never got a report, or a portrait, or a building.

Her name survives. Eunice Smith.

Almost nothing else about her does.

text:
A Prayer for the Victims, Families, and Responders

Heavenly Father, Almighty God,

We come before You with heavy hearts in the wake of this sudden tragedy in Miami. Lord, You are our refuge and strength, a very present help in times of trouble. We lift up the families and loved ones of the five people who lost their lives so unexpectedly. Wrap Your arms of comfort around them as they walk through the valley of the shadow of death, and grant them a peace that surpasses all human understanding.

We pray for those currently fighting for their lives in critical condition, as well as those recovering from their injuries. Lord, be the ultimate Physician over their bodies. Guide the hands of the medical staff, doctors, and nurses caring for them, and bring restoration, healing, and strength to each patient.

We also lift up the firefighters, first responders, and emergency personnel who rushed into danger and confronted such a complex scene. Give them mental, emotional, and physical strength as they process the weight of what they witnessed and continue their crucial work.  In Jesus' name, Amen.

The Hope of Salvation in Jesus Christ

Tragedies like this are a painful reminder of how fragile life is on this earth and how quickly everything can change. Scripture tells us that our earthly lives are like a vapor that appears for a little time and then vanishes away (James 4:14). Because none of us are promised tomorrow, God calls every person to consider where their ultimate hope and eternity lie.

A Broken World in Need of a Savior: The Bible teaches that suffering and death entered the world through sin (Romans 5:12). None of us can save ourselves or guarantee our own future through our own goodness or effort.

God’s Free Gift of Grace: God loved humanity so much that He sent His Son, Jesus Christ, to take the penalty for our sins on the cross and defeat death through His resurrection (John 3:16). Salvation is not earned; it is a free gift of grace offered to everyone (Ephesians 2:8–9).
An Eternal Anchor: For those who place their trust in Jesus, physical death is not the end. Christ promises eternal life in a place where there will be no more pain, sorrow, tragedy, or death (Revelation 21:4).

In moments of shock and grief, the Gospel offers a secure anchor for the soul. Jesus says, "I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die" (John 11:25). May we all turn our hearts to Him today, finding true peace, forgiveness, and the assurance of eternal life.

text:
The Indian opposition is going to have a fun time for a while in the wake of the Delhi demonstrations.  

They will offer themselves as the alternative to the BJP, promising lots of good white collar jobs which Modi has failed to provide.

Maybe they will get power at the centre and in the states.

Then they will find themselves stuck.    How to deliver the promised jobs?   

India's Nehruite economy is extremely hard to change fundamentally.   

Indian factories cannot expand fast because bigger factories cannot lay off workers or hire them easily due to tough labour rules imposed by Nehru.   Unions will defend those rules ruthlessly.  Rahul Gandhi can do nothing about that.  His party opposes a more flexible labour code.

Indian workers are perpetually on strike, deterring domestic and foreign investment.  Rahul Gandhi cannot change that.

Land for factories and infrastructure is hard to buy in India because too much compensation is demanded and there are endless court battles.  Rahul Gandhi cannot change that.   In fact his party helped stop BJP led attempts to make land purchases for industry easier.

High protectionism imposed by Nehru means Indian firms lack the incentive to produce goods of quality good enough to sell in the world market.  So India is poor at exporting goods.  The system benefits Indian industrialists who fund political parties.  Rahul Gandhi cannot change that.

More good jobs in education and health care needs a lot more government spending on both areas.  But India cannot tax rich farmers and so governments do not have the money for such spending.  Nehru perpetuated the no tax of rich farmers policy.  No government dares to abolish it.  Rahul Gandhi can do nothing about it.

So what can Rahul Gandhi offer?

Caste quotas in jobs and education.  This is the opposite of what the upper caste students who are protesting want.

Heigh ho!   

Modi has no answers.    He is on a sticky wicket.

But so is Rahul Gandhi and the opposition.

If they win there will be short term euphoria and then complete disillusionment. 

The cocky Cockroach Party is doomed to disappointment.

No government and no party has easy answers for India.

How strange that no-one in the Indian and foreign press is pointing out these obvious facts!

text:
would winning even feel good if you didn't know what losing felt like?

stay in this online money journey long enough and you turn a bit emotionless.

wake up. 8 hours of work for what seems like nothing. day after day.

you take so many L's that they eventually stop doing anything to you.

nothing in the external world hits anymore because you've already taken so many hits.

you're simply unharmed, by anything out there.

then you finally start to win. it feels like getting something that was always yours.

you wake up to new payment notifications but you feel no emotion.

all the emotion was already felt in the rainy days. nothing compares to that pain.

you'll be around people who take everything so seriously.

something small goes wrong and it's the end of the world. 

you're stood there genuinely wondering "how do you care so much?"

not even judging them. you don't care enough to judge anybody anymore.

just wondering why they put so much energy into meaningless things.

i've gotten the question "are you depressed?" many times.

i know why. i'm quiet most of the time. probably a slightly angry look on my face.

i'm not depressed. i know how to socialize better than them.

could pick anyone in a room and make them my friend within 5 minutes. if i wanted to. 

but... i don't want to. not really into making friends with people who aren't like me.

girls notice this the most. 

they think you're broken. then they start thinking they are the ones who have to "fix" you.

funny, i don't need to be fixed darling.

somehow you end up being the one fixing them. listening to all the things her father did, playing naked psychologist at 1am.

they're all broken. filled with trauma. i like it because they give me more knowledge about human behaviour. 

but i'd be lying if i said i had no trauma. everyone does.

trauma is the thing that led me on this path. the path of being obsessed with becoming better.

difference between me and them is that... i know.

i know my trauma's. started to understand myself on a deeper level.

then pointed all that pain towards my goals. it works.

most of humanity is being driven by their trauma's without knowing they exist.

they just get swallowed by it. a slave to their own unconscious.

her father left her. she's searching for a father figure in me.

i know that. she doesn't. she'll always be searching for a father figure. 

understand that everyone's searching for the thing that's "missing". it's where all the money is.

it's always about filling the hole their life created in them.

looksmaxxers have a deep hole of being insecure about their looks. 

even when they "ascend" nothing changes. 

they're still the same insecure little kids with a better maxilla or something.

why?

because they don't got to know their trauma. they're still a slave to it. 

they look good but still can't talk to a pretty girl. she might notice the penis to eye ratio is wrong.

if you don't get to know your trauma you'll always be searching for the external thing that "fixes" it.

but you'll never find it. because you have to fill it internally.

this is why spending enough time in solitude is good.

you start to understand yourself.

the journey is good for your wallet. but it's also therapy at the same time.

all the lies the world put on you start dissolving.

then the ones you put on yourself. those ones take longer.

and eventually comes what people call "identity change"

but it isn't really change at all.

it seems like you become someone new. but that's not the case.

you're just removing everything fake that sat on top of the true identity.

then you start to realize who you really are. what you really want. what your outlook on life really is.

a stone... a stone is just a stone.

carve it right and it turns into a beautiful artwork people take pictures of.

nothing got added to it. everything that wasn't artwork simply got carved away.

the artwork was already there. but it was hiding between everything that wasn't beautiful.

naturally, high standards come from sitting in solitude. 

very very high standards.

once you've carved something so beautiful you don't accept anything ugly.

your standards get too high for most girls. too high for most guys. too high for most offers.

you're protecting your work. 

people call that arrogance. they can call it what they want.

"be humble. don't have an ego" all that bullshit people throw on you when you level up.

but why should you be humble...

when your whole life before this was the humbling?

don't try to explain this to anyone.

rather dive deep into your own mind and..

explain yourself to yourself.

it's a l4f3styl3 baby.

text:
British AI cloud infrastructure provider Nscale is in talks to raise about $3.5 billion in pre-IPO financing ahead of a planned US listing, sources told Reuters on Friday. The London-based company, founded in 2024, intends to sell as much as $1.5 billion of convertible notes to a group of investors led by New York hedge fund Third Point, and is also seeking about $2 billion from Nvidia. Goldman Sachs is working on the fundraising. The notes are being offered at a double-digit discount to the IPO price, with the discount capped at a $30 billion valuation. Nscale was last valued at $14.6 billion in March after a $2 billion Series C round, and is reportedly eyeing an IPO as soon as this month.

The fundraising comes as demand for GPU-powered compute surges. Nscale owns its own data centers, GPUs and software stack, and last month signed a six-year, $45 billion agreement with Anthropic to rent capacity from its West Virginia campus. The company has told investors its contracted revenue backlog has ballooned to roughly $103 billion from $51 billion a month ago, with projections of about $18.1 billion in annual revenue and $13.6 billion in adjusted earnings on that book. It also struck a separate deal this week to supply at least $3.5 billion of AI cloud capacity to robotics startup Figure, with an intent to scale to over $6 billion, and made an investment in Figure as its preferred compute provider. Nvidia, an investor in both Nscale and Figure, called the partnership an activation of the robotics flywheel.
